articles.title: Newscast - Is RAF Fairford Safe? - BBC Sounds
articles.summary: The US withdraws its bombers from RAF Fairford following last week’s major incident.
articles.body: Today, after the US withdrew its bombers from RAF Fairford, the UK government has insisted the military base is safe. Our security correspondent Frank Gardner explains why the Americans moved the planes back to their home stations. It comes a week after a major incident when police were alerted to three "suspicious vehicles" near the airbase and six arrests were made. Plus, housing protests in Spain have lead to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez calling a snap election. And in France, student protests over the condition of school buildings and staffing have led to clashes with police. Spain correspondent Guy Hedgecoe and Sophie Pedder, the Economists Paris bureau chief explain the context behind the unrest. You can now listen to Newscast on a smart speaker. If you want to listen, just say "Ask BBC Sounds to play Newscast”. It works on most smart speakers. Get in touch with Newscast by emailing newscast@bbc.co.uk or send us a WhatsApp on +44 0330 123 9480. New episodes released every day. If you're in the UK, for more News and Current Affairs podcasts from the BBC, listen on BBC Sounds: Newscast brings you daily analysis of the latest political news stories from the BBC. The presenter was Adam Fleming. It was made by Anna Harris with Cordelia Hemming and Sophie Millward. The social producer was Laura Butler. The technical producer was Ben Andrews. The assistant editor is Chris Gray. The senior news editor is Sam Bonham.

articles.summary: The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from a large demonstration in northern France.
articles.body:
A large crowd with thousands of student protesters has gathered in Lille's Place de la République, in northern France.

Demonstrations are continuing across France on Tuesday against what protesters describe as under-investment in high schools.

The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake, reporting from Lille amid the crowds, can see a strong police presence nearby but no signs of trouble so far.

Some protests over the past week in France have turned violent, as protesters and authorities clashed.

articles.body:
For many children in Yemen, their education is taking place in the shadow of a vicious civil war between forces supporting Yemen's internationally recognised government, which is backed by Saudi Arabia, and the Iran-backed Houthis.

articles.title: Darragh Mackin to represent suspected mob boss Daniel Kinahan
articles.summary: During the first court appearance last August, Kinahan did not have any legal representation.
articles.body:
A solicitor from Northern Ireland is to represent suspected mob boss Daniel Kinahan before the Irish courts in Dublin.

A defence barrister David Perry told the Special Criminal Court on Monday that Darragh Mackin would be Kinahan's defence solicitor.

Kinahan, 49, appeared before court by videolink from Portlaoise Prison for the second time as he faces a charge of directing the activities of a criminal organisation.

During his first court appearance last August, he did not have any legal representation.

Mackin, from Phoenix Law in Belfast, was unable to appear in court in Dublin on Monday as he was attending "other matters elsewhere", which were "unexpected", Perry told the court.

Perry asked if the matter could be pushed back for a week and Judge Caroline Biggs remanded the matter for seven days.

Perry said Kinahan would appear in person at the next court appearance next Monday, adding that it was his preference to appear in person.

Kinahan was extradited from the United Arab Emirates (UAE) on 9 August and flew back to Ireland on board the Irish government's new jet.

He was brought before the Special Criminal Court in Dublin in a high security operation and charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.

Kinahan was arrested in the UAE in April.

He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.

The UK's National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.

Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.

Kinahan faces the charge before the Special Criminal Court, which is a three-judge, non-jury court.

articles.title: Esquerda nunca elegeu governador de SP desde a volta das eleições diretas | G1
articles.standfirst: Desde a redemocratização, estado de São Paulo foi governado primeiro pelo PMDB e depois teve sete vitórias consecutivas do PSDB; partido perdeu o Palácio dos Bandeirantes em 2022 e também encolheu nas eleições municipais de 2024.
articles.summary: Desde a redemocratização, estado de São Paulo foi governado primeiro pelo PMDB e depois teve sete vitórias consecutivas do PSDB; partido perdeu o Palácio dos Bandeirantes em 2022 e também encolheu nas eleições municipais de 2024.
articles.body:
Franco Montoro, primeiro governador eleito diretamente após o regime militar, Geraldo Alckmin e Tarcísio de Freitas — Foto: Montagem g1/Divulgação Alesp/Mateus Bonomi/Estadão Conteúdo/LUIZ RODRIGUES/ATO PRESS/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Desde a retomada das eleições diretas, em 1982, o estado de São Paulo nunca elegeu um governador de um partido tradicionalmente identificado como sendo de esquerda.

Nas últimas quatro décadas, o Palácio dos Bandeirantes foi ocupado por nomes do PMDB , do PSDB e, mais recentemente, do Republicanos .

A primeira eleição direta para governador depois da ditadura militar ocorreu em 1982 e terminou com a vitória de Franco Montoro, do PMDB. Ele foi seguido por Orestes Quércia, também do PMDB, eleito em 1986, e Luiz Antônio Fleury Filho, eleito em 1990, pelo mesmo partido.

Em 1994, Mário Covas venceu a eleição pelo recém-criado PSDB. A partir dali, a legenda passou a dominar as eleições para o governo paulista: foram sete vitórias consecutivas, de Covas, em 1994, a João Doria, em 2018. A sequência terminou em 2022, com a eleição de Tarcísio de Freitas , do Republicanos.

A trajetória foi analisada pelo cientista político Henrique Curi, professor da FESP-SP, em sua dissertação de mestrado pela Unicamp, “Ninho dos Tucanos: o PSDB em São Paulo (1994-2018)”, posteriormente publicada na revista "Opinião Pública".

O estudo investiga a organização e o desempenho eleitoral do partido e aponta que São Paulo teve a maior sequência de vitórias consecutivas de uma legenda para o governo estadual no Brasil no período analisado.

Em entrevista ao g1, Curi ressaltou que a longevidade tucana por quase 30 anos não pode ser explicada apenas pelo perfil do eleitorado paulista. A estrutura partidária nos municípios e a capacidade de formar e manter lideranças também tiveram papel importante (veja abaixo).

Os ex-governadores de São Paulo André Franco Montoro, Orestes Quércia e Luiz Antônio Fleury Filho, todos eleitos pelo antigo PMDB. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Globo

O período entre o fim da ditadura e a ascensão dos tucanos foi marcado pelo PMDB, herdeiro do Movimento Democrático Brasileiro (MDB), criado em 1966 como oposição ao regime militar.

Segundo o Atlas Histórico do Brasil, da Fundação Getulio Vargas (FGV), o MDB surgiu dentro do sistema bipartidário imposto pelo regime, ao lado da Arena, legenda de sustentação do governo.

Durante a ditadura, as eleições para os governos estaduais foram transformadas em indiretas. O AI-3, editado em 1966, estabeleceu que os governadores seriam escolhidos pelas assembleias legislativas. Em São Paulo, Roberto de Abreu Sodré foi eleito dessa maneira naquele ano.

A volta da eleição direta ocorreu em 1982, quando Franco Montoro, então no PMDB, tornou-se o primeiro governador paulista eleito diretamente depois do regime militar. Montoro governou entre 1983 e 1987 e foi sucedido por Quércia, que ficou no cargo até 1991, e Fleury, que governou até 1995.

Em 1988, Montoro foi um dos fundadores do PSDB, ao lado de lideranças como Mário Covas, Fernando Henrique Cardoso e José Serra. A criação da nova sigla ocorreu durante os trabalhos da Assembleia Nacional Constituinte, nos dias 24 e 25 de junho, com forte participação de políticos que haviam pertencido ao PMDB.

A origem do PSDB paulista, portanto, está ligada a uma dissidência do partido que havia governado o estado no período de redemocratização. Nos anos seguintes, os tucanos construíram uma estrutura própria para ampliar sua presença eleitoral nos municípios.

Foto de arquivo de 12/03/2018 do ex- governador de São Paulo, Geraldo Alckmin — Foto: DIDA SAMPAIO/ESTADÃO CONTEÚDO

Uma explicação frequentemente levantada para a sequência de vitórias tucanas é a de que São Paulo teria um eleitorado de centro-direita, com forte presença da classe média e identificação com o PSDB. Para Curi, porém, essa interpretação não é suficiente.

“São Paulo seria um eleitorado de centro-direita, classe média, identificação partidária com o PSDB, mas ela é insuficiente. A explicação mais robusta, que eu considero, é por uma via organizacional e institucional do partido ”, afirma o cientista político.

Na avaliação do pesquisador, um dos principais fatores foi a capacidade de organização do partido nos municípios. A Executiva estadual acompanhava a atuação dos diretórios nas 645 cidades paulistas e mantinha coordenadores regionais nas 63 regiões de governo do estado.

“O PSDB de São Paulo contava com uma Executiva estadual que era capaz de monitorar os 645 municípios. Ele apostou sua organização nessa interiorização, nos diretórios municipais, em vez de ter comissões provisórias, como os outros partidos faziam no resto do país”, diz Curi.

O partido também mantinha um sistema interno, conhecido como “intranet tucana”, para acompanhar o desempenho das estruturas municipais. O mecanismo permitia identificar demandas locais, avaliar resultados eleitorais e decidir sobre o apoio oferecido aos diretórios.

“Isso permitia captar demandas locais, recrutar lideranças e premiar e punir diretórios. O desempenho eleitoral do partido em cada município seguia métricas que eram passíveis de premiação e punição. Variavam desde o maior suporte durante o mandato até o apoio durante as campanhas nas eleições seguintes”, afirma.

Segundo o pesquisador, apesar da atuação local, os diretórios permaneciam sob acompanhamento da direção estadual. O desempenho também podia influenciar a permanência de seus dirigentes.

Outro fator foi a capacidade de atrair políticos com diferentes níveis de experiência eleitoral. O PSDB recrutava tanto pessoas que nunca haviam disputado uma eleição quanto políticos veteranos.

“Historicamente, o PSDB era o partido em São Paulo que mais atraía debutantes, pessoas que nunca se candidataram anteriormente. E, além de atrair os debutantes, atraía os veteranos também, que eram pessoas que já tinham se candidatado”, diz Curi.

O pesquisador também destaca a continuidade entre as lideranças tucanas. Nomes como Mário Covas, Geraldo Alckmin, José Serra e Fernando Henrique Cardoso atuaram em diferentes momentos da trajetória da legenda, sem que a direção política dependesse de um único líder.

Para Curi, a combinação entre organização interna, recrutamento de lideranças e continuidade política ajuda a explicar por que o partido conseguiu manter o governo paulista por tanto tempo.

Palácio dos Bandeirantes, sede do governo de São Paulo, no Morumbi, Zona Sul de São Paulo. — Foto: Divulgação/GESP

A presença municipal não se limitava à organização dos diretórios. Ela também era parte da estratégia eleitoral do PSDB. Em 1996, o então governador Mário Covas orientou o partido a ampliar o número de candidaturas ao Executivo municipal.

Segundo o levantamento de Curi, o PSDB passou de cinco prefeituras conquistadas em 1988 para 50 em 1992 e chegou a 221 em 1996, crescimento de 342% entre as duas últimas eleições. Os dados foram elaborados pelo autor a partir de informações do Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE).

Naquele ano, o partido lançou candidatos a prefeito em 446 municípios, o equivalente a 69% das cidades paulistas. A estratégia foi ampliada nos anos seguintes: entre 2000 e 2016, o PSDB apresentou candidatos a vereador, em média, em 98,7% dos municípios do estado.

A avaliação do desempenho municipal, porém, não se limitava ao número de prefeituras conquistadas. O partido também considerava a população que estava sob a administração de seus prefeitos e a participação nas alianças eleitorais.

“O PSDB paulista media o sucesso pela população governada”, afirma Curi.

Com o tempo, a legenda também passou a recorrer mais às coligações em cidades menores, em vez de necessariamente lançar um candidato próprio a prefeito. Segundo o pesquisador, essa mudança esteve ligada à estratégia de Geraldo Alckmin de construir alianças com o maior número possível de partidos e municípios, também como forma de preparar o apoio à candidatura presidencial de 2006.

A organização municipal também servia para avaliar o trabalho dos dirigentes. De acordo com Curi, a Executiva estadual utilizava critérios formais de desempenho, que incluíam desde a ausência de candidatura própria a prefeito até a conquista de mais de 10% dos votos ou a eleição de um vereador. Diretórios com resultados considerados insatisfatórios podiam ter seus dirigentes substituídos.

Curi também apontou em seu artigo a força do PSDB nas coligações municipais. Entre 2000 e 2016, o partido participou, em média, de 95,6% das disputas majoritárias municipais paulistas e esteve na cabeça da chapa em 54,8% das candidaturas de que participou.

A legenda também atraiu políticos de outras siglas. Segundo o estudo, em 2016, 26,7% dos vereadores veteranos que disputavam a eleição haviam entrado no PSDB, enquanto 7,2% haviam deixado o partido. Entre prefeitos veteranos, 38,3% entraram na sigla e 10% saíram.

Para o cientista político, a presença nos municípios foi fundamental para sustentar a influência do PSDB no estado e ampliar sua participação nas disputas eleitorais.

Por que a esquerda nunca venceu o governo paulista?

A ausência de um governador de um partido tradicionalmente identificado à esquerda desde a retomada das eleições diretas também está relacionada, segundo Curi, às diferenças entre o desempenho eleitoral na capital e no interior e à dificuldade de construir uma estrutura partidária nos municípios.

“Historicamente, o PT é mais forte na capital”, afirma o cientista político. Segundo ele, o partido encontra mais dificuldades no interior, onde há municípios industrializados, cidades médias e pequenas cidades prósperas, além de regiões marcadas pela presença do agronegócio e pelo antipetismo.

Para Curi, essa diferença ajuda a explicar por que o desempenho do PT na capital nem sempre se traduz em vitória nas eleições estaduais.

“O segundo turno no estado de São Paulo evidencia um clássico Holanda na Copa do Mundo para o PT, que joga como nunca e perde como sempre”, diz o pesquisador.

Além do perfil do eleitorado, Curi destaca a dificuldade histórica do PT para ampliar sua presença no interior e acessar as estruturas políticas municipais. Nesse espaço, o PMDB havia construído uma presença importante antes de o PSDB assumir o protagonismo. Mais recentemente, o PSD também passou a ampliar sua atuação nas cidades do interior.

O pesquisador cita como exemplo a estratégia tucana de buscar o apoio de prefeitos do PMDB, inclusive com a realização de um evento com Franco Montoro para atrair essas lideranças. Segundo ele, a força dos partidos já estabelecidos dificultou a entrada do PT nesses municípios.

Para Curi, a ausência de uma estrutura municipal comparável à de seus adversários e os obstáculos impostos por forças partidárias já estabelecidas ajudam a explicar por que o PT não conseguiu ocupar o mesmo espaço no interior paulista.

A mudança na polarização e a crise interna

João Doria e Rodrigo Garcia (PSDB) eleitos governador e vice governador de São Paulo em 2018 — Foto: Divulgação/PSDB

A eleição de 2018 já havia mostrado sinais de mudança. Apesar da vitória de João Doria, aquele foi o pleito mais disputado para o governo paulista até então dentro da trajetória tucana, com a menor diferença de votos entre os dois candidatos no segundo turno desde a primeira vitória do PSDB, em 1994. Curi também destacou naquele momento o crescimento do PSB-SP nas disputas municipais e estaduais.

Ao g1 , o pesquisador apontou três fatores para explicar o encolhimento do PSDB nos anos seguintes: a mudança no protagonismo da polarização política, a crise interna e a perda de lideranças e a saída do governo estadual.

O primeiro fator está relacionado à mudança na disputa política nacional. Entre 1994 e 2014, o PSDB ocupou o principal polo de oposição ao PT. A partir de 2018, esse espaço passou a ser ocupado por Jair Bolsonaro.

“O PSDB era o polo antipetista do país que disputava com o PT. Em 2018, esse papel, esse polo migrou para Jair Bolsonaro”, afirma Curi.

Naquele período, o PSDB paulista também se aproximou do bolsonarismo. Para o pesquisador, essa aproximação contribuiu para reduzir a identidade própria da legenda. O rompimento entre Doria e Bolsonaro durante a pandemia de Covid-19 deixou o partido em uma posição mais difícil diante de parte do eleitorado.

“Quando o Doria rompeu com o Bolsonaro na pandemia, o partido ficou meio sem lugar, ficou meio perdido frente ao eleitorado”, diz Curi.

Segundo ele, a legenda continuou enfrentando rejeição entre eleitores de esquerda e passou a ser acusada de traição por setores da direita após o afastamento do então presidente.

O segundo fator foi a perda de lideranças e a crise interna. Curi cita a saída de quadros que haviam construído suas trajetórias no PSDB, como Geraldo Alckmin, Floriano Pesaro, Mara Gabrilli e Carlos Sampaio, além das dificuldades de Doria para sustentar sua candidatura à Presidência da República, apesar de ter vencido as prévias internas.

O pesquisador também menciona a escolha de Rodrigo Garcia para disputar o governo paulista em 2022. Garcia havia chegado recentemente ao PSDB, vindo do DEM, e não tinha experiência anterior em uma disputa eleitoral para o Executivo.

Para Curi, o partido perdeu parte da coesão que havia caracterizado sua direção e sua capacidade de reunir diferentes lideranças.

O terceiro fator foi a perda do governo estadual em 2022. Segundo o pesquisador, o comando do Palácio dos Bandeirantes era importante para sustentar a estrutura partidária nos municípios, tanto pelo acompanhamento dos diretórios quanto pelo apoio político às lideranças locais.

“O partido governador era um dos pontos que conseguia turbinar o monitoramento do partido e ter essa máquina municipal. Perdeu o Palácio dos Bandeirantes em 2022, perdeu esse motor”, afirma.

O encolhimento nas eleições municipais de 2024

Mapa das cidades de São Paulo vencidas por cada partido em 2024. — Foto: Reprodução/g1

Nas eleições municipais de 2024, o PSDB perdeu espaço no estado de São Paulo. O número de prefeituras comandadas pelo partido caiu de 173 para 21.

Enquanto os tucanos encolheram, outras siglas ampliaram sua presença nos municípios paulistas. O PSD terminou a eleição com 206 prefeitos eleitos em 645 municípios, tornando-se o partido com maior número de prefeituras no estado. Na sequência apareceram o PL, com 104 prefeitos, e o Republicanos, com 84. O MDB ficou na quarta posição.

A legenda também não elegeu prefeito em nenhuma capital e ficou sem representação na Câmara Municipal de São Paulo.

A queda no número de prefeituras ocorreu dois anos depois de o PSDB perder o governo estadual. Para Curi, a perda do Palácio dos Bandeirantes, a crise interna e as mudanças na polarização política ajudam a explicar a redução da presença tucana nos municípios e o enfraquecimento da estrutura que havia sustentado a hegemonia do partido por 28 anos.

articles.title: Yemen forces claim key gains near Bab al-Mandeb: What’s the latest?
articles.summary: The internationally recognised government retakes territories from the Houthis as fighting rages on the western coast.
articles.body:
Yemeni government forces say they have seized several strategic positions near the Bab al-Mandeb strait from the Iran-aligned Houthis, as fighting intensifies along the country’s western coast.

In response, the Houthis, an armed group also known by its Arabic name Ansar Allah, or Supporters of God, have claimed attacks on airports, oil infrastructure and military sites in Saudi Arabia.

The latest offensive by the Saudi-backed Yemeni government army follows major Houthi gains in September, when the group swept over the country’s Red Sea coast, capturing the strategic port city of Mocha and territory around the Bab al-Mandeb, one of the world’s most important shipping routes.

Rashad al-Alimi, chairman of Yemen’s Presidential Leadership Council, has said the government’s new operation – Dawn of Yemen – announced on Sunday, aims to retake all remaining Houthi-held territory, including the capital, Sanaa, which the group has controlled since 2014, when the war first started.

So, where does the fighting stand, and what could happen next?

Southwestern Yemen has witnessed the heaviest fighting, particularly along the Red Sea coast and around Taiz.

Yemen’s government forces backed by Saudi Arabia said they, together with the Popular Resistance Forces, had taken control of the al-Manzara, al-Ashari and Dhiban mountains in Haifan, south of Taiz.

Earlier, Yemeni government forces claimed they had captured Mocha and Dhubab, both in Taiz governorate, as well as positions around Bab al-Mandeb, in a rapid Saudi-backed counteroffensive.

Government forces, supported by heavy Saudi air strikes, reached the outskirts of Mocha on Monday as Houthi fighters retreated towards the highlands, four government sources told the Reuters news agency.

Yemen’s Defence Ministry later said the city had fallen.

Without revealing any specifics, a Houthi military spokesman on Tuesday said the group remained in control of its battlefield gains and described reports from its opponents as “fabricated heroics”.

Al Jazeera has not independently verified the full extent of the government’s territorial gains.

Fernando Carvajal, a former United Nations Security Council adviser on Yemen, said the battle for Mocha will be key to the next phase of fighting.

“This will be a vital sign for us if the Yemeni government forces, led by the Southern Giants and other southern forces, can hold this city. Because, at the moment, when you look at the battle plan, Mocha is surrounded by Houthis from all three sides, and you have the Red Sea,” he told Al Jazeera.

“So, we need to wait just a little bit more to see if indeed the government forces can hold this city and then use it as a staging point to take on the Houthis on other fronts.”

The fighting has also extended northwards along the Red Sea coast to Hodeidah, which has been under Houthi control since October 2014. The Houthis had captured Sanaa weeks before that.

The Saudi-led coalition’s spokesman, Major-General Turki al-Maliki, said its naval forces struck Houthi “military targets” in the Hodeidah governorate, including weapons depots and facilities used to store explosive-laden boats and naval mines.

Al-Maliki said the operation “thwarted a planned attack” on waterways in the southern Red Sea. The coalition also said its naval forces had carried out a military operation in Hodeidah.

Meanwhile, the Houthis said their forces carried out dozens of strikes on Tuesday targeting “enemy” reinforcements east of al-Jawf governorate, resulting in an unspecified number of casualties.

The Houthis have simultaneously stepped up attacks on Saudi Arabia, according to Houthi-affiliated media. They targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh, an Aramco refinery in Rabigh, Abha airport and the Khamis Mushait military base with missiles and drones, as well as sites in the southern Saudi cities of Najran and Jazan.

Saudi Arabia has yet to comment on all those specific claims.

However, on Tuesday, the Saudi General Authority of Civil Aviation said the King Abdullah Bin ⁠⁠⁠⁠Abdulaziz international ⁠⁠⁠⁠airport in Jazan and the Najran international ‌‌‌‌airport were targeted in two attacks on Monday evening, causing three minor injuries.

Later in the day, the Houthis claimed another attack on a Saudi airport, this time targeting Abha International Airport in Asir Province, with a ballistic missile.

Riyadh has yet to confirm the alleged attack.

What is the humanitarian situation on the ground?

The escalation is worsening what was already one of the world’s gravest humanitarian crises.

The International Organization for Migration said on Monday that more than 184,000 people have been displaced since the war resumed.

According to the World Health Organization, the latest fighting has killed at least 959 people and wounded more than 4,200.

The fighting has also disrupted healthcare in the war-devastated country.

“Yemen’s latest escalation is pushing an already fragile health system towards breaking point,” warned Annette Heinzelmann, WHO’s emergency director for the eastern Mediterranean region.

The escalation has drawn a response from Saudi Arabia’s regional allies, with Turkiye and Pakistan agreeing to rapidly deploy military forces and capabilities to Saudi Arabia under the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement.

Signed in August, the pact is designed to strengthen collective deterrence and stipulates that an armed attack against Saudi Arabia, Pakistan or Turkiye will be regarded as an attack on all three.

The United States, one of Saudi Arabia’s closest allies, is providing intelligence support to Riyadh, according to media reports.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday Saudi Arabia and the Yemeni government had “a right to defend themselves”.

“And obviously the Yemeni forces are going to try to retake territory that they were ousted from,” he told reporters.

Military vehicles travel along a road during what Yemeni government forces say was an advance against the Iran-backed Houthis, near Dhubab, Taiz governorate [Handout/Southern Giants Brigades via Reuters]

articles.title: Malaysia’s Anwar to host Myanmar leader as repatriations near 10,000
articles.summary: Myanmar President Min Aung Hlaing to visit Kuala Lumpur ‘in the next few days’, Anwar Ibrahim says.
articles.body:
Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim says about 10,000 ⁠people have been sent back to Myanmar since January, despite safety warnings by human rights groups and the United Nations refugee agency.

Anwar told parliament on Tuesday that a number of those deported were sent back by ⁠planes arranged by the Myanmar government, while nearly 1,500 were returned by sea last week as part of a bilateral arrangement.

Anwar acknowledged concerns by rights groups and lawmakers over the ⁠potential safety risks faced by those being repatriated, especially those from the Rohingya Muslim minority, but said Myanmar authorities had given ⁠assurances that they would not be harmed ⁠upon their return.

“The conditions that we placed on Myanmar is that they must bring home their citizens,” Anwar said. “Secondly, it is that they treat their people fairly so ‌that there are no abuses, coercion or rights violations.”

Anwar said he would continue to discuss the ‌matter ‌with Myanmar’s President Min Aung Hlaing, who is due to visit Kuala Lumpur “in the next few days”.

The visit is part of a diplomatic push for legitimacy by the Myanmar leader, whose 2021 coup plunged Myanmar into civil war and who led a 2017 military crackdown that forced hundreds of thousands of Rohingya people to flee the country.

Malaysia insists all returnees agreed to repatriation, but rights monitors have raised concerns that Myanmar refugees had little choice.

The UN High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR) said last week that its staff was not allowed to meet the Myanmar nationals to confirm whether their decisions to return “were genuinely free and informed”.

The deportations come amid escalating raids on refugee communities in Malaysia by immigration officials, which led to the detention of more than 50,000 refugees in 2026.

Rohingya make up the majority of Myanmar refugees and asylum seekers in Malaysia, but it remains unclear how many members of the persecuted group were among those deported.

Malaysia took in about 193,000 refugees from Myanmar, according to UN data.

While Malaysia is not a party to the UN Refugee Convention and treats refugees as undocumented migrants, it is home to about 215,600 refugees and asylum seekers registered with the UNHCR.

Myanmar has been accused of committing genocide against the Rohingya. Earlier this year, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) opened its first genocide case it has heard in full in more than a decade.

The UNHCR and rights groups said returnees could face persecution and forced military conscription in an active war zone. Myanmar has been embroiled in a civil war since the military seized power from the elected government in 2021.

The war has killed more than 100,000 people since the coup, according to the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project.

images.caption: Myanmar nationals to be repatriated from Malaysia sit inside a bus, at Lumut, Malaysia, September 29, 2026 [Hasnoor Hussain/Reuters]

articles.title: Coco Gauff hits out at racist abuse after replayed point in Beijing draws backlash
articles.summary: Coco Gauff said she had received an “insane” amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-time Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open on Monday in a match where a replayed point set off an online backlash.
articles.body: Coco Gauff said she had received an “insane” amount of racial abuse on social media after the two-time Grand Slam champion beat local teenager Sun Xinran at the China Open on Monday in a match where a replayed point set off an online backlash. The American won 7-5, 6-1 to reach the fourth round, but was targeted after stopping play during a crucial point in the first set, raising her hand to complain about a flickering advertising board just as Sun was about to put away a winner. After a video review, the umpire ordered the point to be replayed. Gauff won the replayed point and held serve for 5-5 before cruising to victory against the Chinese 16-year-old. Gauff, 22, said she had received a barrage of abusive messages on social media after the match. “You can dislike me or disagree about what happened without being racist,” Gauff, who is Black, said on X early Tuesday in reply to a post containing a racial slur. “The amount of racist comments/direct messages I’ve received in the last few hours is insane. “Lastly, I’m not a cheater or a thief.” Reuters has contacted the WTA, the governing body of women’s tennis, and tournament organizers in Beijing for comment. The WTA has made efforts to tackle the issue of online abuse by introducing an AI-powered system that monitors thousands of players and officials on social media. A study by the WTA and World Tennis showed players were subjected to over 12,000 abusive posts and messages on social media in 2025, up from 8,000 posts a year earlier. Gauff also explained that she was following the rules when she challenged the point. Players are allowed to request video reviews of select judgment calls, including claims that a distraction may have interfered with play. The American said she had spoken to Sun about the point at the end of the match. “Xinran’s an incredible talent and player, I apologized for the situation at the end of the match and she completely understood,” she wrote. “I didn’t like to see her so emotional as I’ve been there and I really understand what it’s like but this is the beginning of an incredible career. It was an honor to share the court in front of her home crowd.”

articles.title: Small inflatable boats 'set for people smugglers' seized at East Midlands Airport
articles.summary: The National Crime Agency says it is the first time the detection of small boat equipment has been made in air freight.
articles.body:
Officers have seized 25 inflatable boats reportedly destined to be shipped to cross-Channel people smugglers.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) said the boats - about nine metres in length - were spotted in pallets on an air freight shipment being moved from Turkey to the Netherlands.

The shipment went through a freight hub at East Midlands Airport on the way, allowing NCA and Border Force to intercept on Friday.

NCA officers added this was the second time a large consignment of small boat equipment had been seized in the UK in 2026, but the first time such a detection had been made in air freight.

In July, 25 boats and 25 engines were seized in a maritime consignment at Felixstowe in Suffolk. The boat carrying them had stopped there on the way to Germany.

Home Office figures show more than 20,000 migrants have crossed the Channel in small boats so far this year.

A total of 609 people arrived in eight boats on Monday - taking the figure for 2026 to 20,478 people. This is substantially lower than for the same period last year.

The NCA said, had the latest shipment made its way into the hands of people smugglers, "each could have been used to transport around 70 people across the Channel".

The NCA estimated the boats could have been used to move up to 1,700 migrants.

NCA deputy director of investigations Craig Turner said: "We continue to target groups or individuals directly involved in the supply of boats and engines used in the Channel for people smuggling.

"This work is happening both overseas, with international partners, and here in the UK. So far it has led to the seizure of in excess of 1,600 boats and engines, denying their use to criminal networks.

"Our assessment is that this is having an impact, driving up the cost of boats and engines, making it more difficult to get them to the coast and eating into the profits of the criminal gangs involved.

"I've no doubt the boats we've seized here would have ended up being used to risk the lives of a huge number of people in the Channel had we not stepped in. Our investigation continues."

Minister for border security and asylum Anna Turley added: "This seizure of 25 small boats delivers yet another blow to the evil smuggling gangs.

"Disruptions to supply lines like these are happening more than ever before as we bear down on the illegal and dangerous crossings."

The NCA said about 100 investigations into gangs involved in organisation immigration crime were ongoing.

Adam Berry, branch commander for the alternative disruption team, confirmed it was the first time it had made a seizure of air freight in the UK.

"These boats are so dangerous," he said. "We have sadly seen so many deaths in the Channel recently, and it's because they are just purely constructed to get across as cheaply and as flimsily as possible.

"What we can see when we get the boats and we blow the boats up is that there's distinctive shapes and types of them.

"There's a distinctive transom - which is the bit where the engine sits - and then you've got how many chambers they are, the construction of them and other key bits.

"We can look at boats that have arrived and we can compare them to these and prove that these boats are the exact boats that we have seen in the Channel."

articles.title: Carbon tracking tower put on Caerlaverock saltmarsh
articles.summary: It will track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by the saltmarsh on the Solway Firth.
articles.body:
New technology has been installed to track how much carbon is being taken out of the atmosphere by Scotland's largest saltmarsh.

The flux tower has been put in place at Caerlaverock on the Solway Firth.

About 85% of UK saltmarshes have been lost since the mid-19th Century as land has been reclaimed from the sea for agriculture, development or coastal flood defences, degraded through pollution or eroded by rising sea levels.

Corallie Hunt, coastal habitats adviser for NatureScot, said the installation of the first saltmarsh flux tower in Scotland marked an "important milestone".

The project is a partnership between UK Centre for Ecology and Hydrology (UKCEH), the Scottish government, NatureScot, and WWF-UK.

"By measuring carbon exchange in real time, it will strengthen our understanding of the carbon storage potential of saltmarshes and the value of protecting and restoring these habitats," said Hunt.

UKCEH wetland scientist Annette Burden said the Solway flux tower was the most northerly addition to a network around the UK coast.

"The data collected will aid in understanding the role saltmarsh plays in climate mitigation, provide evidence for saltmarsh inclusion in the UK Greenhouse Gas (GHG) Inventory, which in turn will strengthen calls to safeguard and restore this valuable habitat," she said.

In addition to supporting biodiversity and providing natural flood protection, the plants covering the marshes draw down carbon dioxide through photosynthesis and can also trap carbon-rich sediments in their roots and stems on the incoming tide.

Tom Brook, ocean conservation specialist at WWF said: "The Solway is an extraordinary place for nature.

"From thousands of migratory birds that depend on these wetlands to the rare natterjack toad, the saltmarsh supports an incredible variety of wildlife.

"It's also working hard for people too – helping to absorb wave energy and reduce the impacts of flooding and storm surges.

"The data gathered by the tower will help us better understand and champion the value of these remarkable coastal habitats."

articles.title: FlyDubai flight incident: Did aviation miss the insider-threat warning?
articles.summary: The FlyDubai incident has raised a difficult question for the aviation industry: what happens when the threat is already inside the cockpit?
articles.body: The FlyDubai incident has raised a difficult question for the aviation industry: what happens when the threat is already inside the cockpit?Aviation safety expert Captain Amit Singh believes the incident should be a wake-up call for everyone - especially the global aviation industry. In an interview with me on Times Axis channel, he pointed to gaps in information sharing, pilot background checks and the growing danger of insider threats.The incident took place on a FlyDubai flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv. The co-pilot, an Omani national, attacked the captain while the aircraft was in flight.Reports have suggested that the co-pilot may have intended to take control of the aircraft and crash it in Israel.Singh said the sequence of events was consistent with such a possibility. His assessment was that the attack on the captain could have been an attempt to take control of the aircraft. When that failed, the co-pilot may have tried to bring the aircraft down.These are questions for investigators to establish. The cockpit voice recorder and flight data recorder will be crucial in reconstructing what happened.But there is another question that Singh believes needs urgent attention. How did the warning against this pilot get lost when he moved from one country and airline to another?Reports have said the pilot had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about extremist views. He later worked in other countries before joining FlyDubai. Singh said this raises questions about how far back airlines and aviation authorities look when checking a pilot's history. A pilot may move from one country to another and obtain a new licence. Does a new employer get the complete picture?“If somebody, say, his licence was suspended in Oman, then he goes to Morocco, he gets a new licence, he gets a Moroccan licence. And then he shifts somewhere else, he gets a third-country licence, then he comes to Dubai. So Dubai will only check the past licence, not the past three or four licences. So this is a matter of debate.”The larger problem, he argued, is the lack of seamless information sharing across jurisdictions. That is where the concept of the insider threat becomes important.The International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) issued an Insider Threat Toolkit in 2022. Singh pointed out that an insider does not necessarily mean someone who has entered an airport illegally. It could be a baggage handler, a member of the catering staff, cabin crew, an engineer or even a pilot.All of them have legitimate access to sensitive areas and systems. The industry, he said, has known about such risks for years. There have been cases involving insiders taking control of aircraft or helping explosives get on board.But he feels that a separate regulation cannot exist for every possible threat. The industry also needs a culture in which small warning signs are reported and information is shared.A disturbing social media post may appear insignificant. So may a warning issued to an employee. But repeated incidents can form a pattern.The challenge is making sure that pattern reaches the people responsible for security. Singh described these early signals as “murmurs”. The question is whether aviation is listening to them.The 30-second windowThere was another extraordinary element to the FlyDubai incident. The captain managed to open the cockpit door after being attacked. Passengers then entered the cockpit and restrained the co-pilot. One passenger, identified as an Israeli plumber, took the controls while the aircraft was in a steep descent. Singh estimates that the aircraft was descending at around 25,000 feet per minute - about ten times the normal rate of descent, according to his assessment. The aircraft was under enormous stress. The passengers needed to act quickly. According to him, the aircraft had only seconds before it would have hit the ground. Therefore, the captain's decision to open the door was critical. That decision may have saved the aircraft. But Singh believes there was something else unusual about the combination of people on that flight.“The pilot was an Indian and the passengers were Israeli. Had there been different nationalities, the outcome would have been different,” he said.Singh said the captain's resilience and his faith helped him push through his injuries and reach the cockpit door. He also believes the Israeli citizens’ military training and their instinct to respond quickly helped prevent the aircraft from crashing. He called it their “survival mode”. The point, Singh said, was not that the passengers knew how to fly. It was that they did not freeze. The distinction is important. They were not flying the aircraft in the conventional sense. They were responding to an extreme emergency with almost no time to think. And that is what makes those 30 seconds so important.What happens next?Videos recorded by passengers have already fuelled speculation about what happened inside the aircraft.Singh identified one detail that could be significant: emergency lights appear to come on during the incident. Those lights can be activated during a loss of electrical power. In Amit Singh's view, this raises the possibility that both the aircraft's engines may have temporarily lost power or may have been deliberately shut down.That cannot be established from the videos alone. The flight data recorder should provide a much clearer picture. But the larger lesson may extend well beyond FlyDubai.Aviation security relies on layers of checks. Licences are checked. Backgrounds are checked. Security clearances are issued.But an individual's history can cross several countries and employers. A single database may not capture all of it. Singh believes aviation needs better information sharing, continuous background checks and technology – especially AI and biometrics.People working in aviation must also feel they can report unusual behaviour without being punished for raising a concern.The aviation industry cannot afford to ignore this question: Are we still looking for terrorists outside the system when the next threat may already have legitimate access from inside it?Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: One fraternity house, 7 accused men, no criminal charges: Cornell rape case explained in 5 questions
articles.summary: What happened at a Cornell University fraternity house on a night in October 2024 is back under the spotlight nearly two years later, raising troubling
articles.body: What happened at a Cornell University fraternity house on a night in October 2024 is back under the spotlight nearly two years later, raising troubling questions about sexual assault, campus accountability and the limits of the justice system.The case involves a Cornell student known in court records as “Jane Doe”, who accused seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity of sexually assaulting her after she became heavily intoxicated and, according to her account, was given ketamine.She reported the alleged assault to Cornell police weeks later, but no criminal charges were filed at the time. Cornell conducted its own disciplinary investigation, eventually expelling two of the men and imposing lesser sanctions on others.The case has now resurfaced after Doe sued Cornell and the men, triggering renewed scrutiny of the university's handling of the allegations. New York Governor Kathy Hochul ordered an independent review of Cornell's response and appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to take over the criminal investigation.What happened at Cornell fraternity house?According to Doe's account to investigators and allegations in her lawsuit, she went to the Chi Phi fraternity house on October 19, 2024, to meet Matthew Ingalls, a man she had been interested in romantically.She told investigators she initially arrived with an intoxication level she described as about five out of 10 after drinking during the evening. At the fraternity house, she said Ingalls asked whether she wanted to have a threesome with Jonathan Newell.She alleged that alcohol and ketamine were then involved and that, as the night progressed, other men entered the room and engaged in sexual acts with her while she was incapacitated.The university records also describe a Snapchat message allegedly sent by Newell encouraging other fraternity members to enter the bedroom while Doe was undressed. Cornell's disciplinary summaries later said Ingalls was responsible for sexual assault and that he had manipulated, exploited and endangered Doe for his own interests and the entertainment of others.Doe has described the experience in stark terms. According to records reviewed by The Associated Press, she told Cornell investigators: “I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in.”But the seven men have denied wrongdoing. Records also show that some of the accused described the sexual activity and drug use as consensual. Cornell's disciplinary panel did not find all seven responsible for sexual assault.What did Cornell's investigation find?Cornell conducted a separate disciplinary process from the criminal investigation.The university's three-member Title IX panel met over 12 days in May 2025. According to disciplinary summaries obtained by The New York Times, the panel reached different conclusions about the seven men and imposed different sanctions.Two men - Ingalls and Newell - were expelled.Ingalls was found responsible for sexual assault. Newell was also accused of sexual assault and was expelled, with the disciplinary records noting, among other allegations, that Doe told police he had struck her during intercourse and manipulated her into ingesting ketamine.Two others, Winston Lee and Gillio Lopes, were suspended. Lee received a two-year suspension followed by disciplinary probation, while Lopes received a three-semester suspension and two years of probation. Both were also ordered to have no contact with Doe and complete education and reflection requirements.Diego Sarabia, who had already graduated, was declared persona non grata and barred from campus for three years.The remaining two, Scott Norris and Scott Kretzschmar, received restrictions including no-contact orders, educational requirements and reflection papers. Kretzschmar was not found responsible for sexual assault but was found responsible for the lesser offence of attempted sexual exploitation. His lawyer said he was “never accused of, nor found responsible for, rape.”The sanctions ranged from expulsion to comparatively lighter disciplinary measures. Cornell has declined to provide further details, citing student privacy laws.Why is Cornell facing criticism?For many students, the central question is not only what happened inside the fraternity house but also whether the university did enough after Doe reported it.The case sparked protests on campus, with students demanding greater transparency and accountability. Demonstrators carried signs reading “support survivors, expel rapists” and “Justice 4 every Jane Doe”, while some called for Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff to resign.The protests followed the emergence of detailed records from Cornell's investigation and Doe's lawsuit.Cornell President Kotlikoff acknowledged the seriousness of the allegations, saying Doe's account “raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanization and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use.” He backed an independent review and promised a commitment to “finding the answers our community deserves.”Why were there no criminal charges in 2024?This is one of the most important distinctions in the case: Cornell's disciplinary findings and the criminal investigation are separate processes.Doe reported the alleged assault to Cornell police in November 2024. Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten initially declined to pursue criminal charges after reviewing a police summary of her interview.Van Houten later said Cornell police had not provided him with key information, including a transcript in which Doe reportedly said she was “100% confident I was raped.” He said the material he initially received suggested that she had consented to some sexual activity and was intoxicated, but not necessarily to the degree of being legally incapacitated.He subsequently reopened the investigation, saying that cases sometimes have to be reconsidered when additional evidence emerges.The question of intoxication is legally significant. According to the supplied reporting, New York law distinguishes between being intoxicated and being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent. That distinction can affect whether prosecutors can establish the elements required for a rape charge.Van Houten has maintained that state law limited what he could prosecute based solely on Doe's allegation that she was too incapacitated to consent.Doe's civil lawsuit brought renewed attention to the case and included allegations that Van Houten said he had not previously seen.Hochul said she had lost confidence in the local prosecutor's handling of the matter and criticised what she described as failures by institutions that were supposed to protect Doe. She ordered an independent review of Cornell's handling of the case.The governor then appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor with the authority to bring criminal charges. James has said the investigation could take months and that there would be no predetermined outcome.That means the renewed criminal inquiry is still an investigation, not a finding that the accused men committed crimes.What does the recorded phone call reveal?Another piece of evidence highlighted in the reporting is a phone call Doe recorded with one of the men shortly before she went to Cornell police.According to ABC News, the man said that after dancing with Doe, he suggested a three-person sexual encounter and maintained that she agreed. During the call, Doe tried to identify other men she said later entered the room. The man suggested that both of them might be remembering something incorrectly.At one point, according to ABC's account, Doe told him: “What y'all did would be classified as gang rape.” She had earlier alleged that she was too intoxicated to consent.The recording is part of the broader body of material surrounding the case, but it does not by itself resolve the competing accounts of what happened.The case has turned into a wider debate on Cornell's handling of sexual assault allegations.At a Cornell Student Assembly meeting, students discussed their experiences with sexual violence and the university's response. One student, Jane Wang, said that after filing a Title IX case following an earlier alleged assault, she encountered extensive paperwork, little guidance and no follow-up about the outcome.Student organisations have called for an independent review of Cornell's handling of the Doe case and changes to sexual-assault policies. Cornell's fraternity presidents also voted to cancel social events for a weekend following the allegations.Meanwhile, the controversy has expanded beyond Cornell. Hochul has said she supports changing New York's sexual assault law concerning people who are too intoxicated to consent, adding another dimension to the debate over how such cases are prosecuted.Three separate tracks now matter in the Cornell case: the civil lawsuit, the university's disciplinary findings and the renewed criminal investigation.Cornell has already imposed disciplinary sanctions on the seven men, including two expulsions, but its panel did not find all seven responsible for sexual assault. The men have denied wrongdoing, and some have disputed Doe's account.The criminal case is different. James' appointment as special prosecutor means investigators will now examine the evidence afresh, without a predetermined outcome. Whether criminal charges are ultimately brought remains unresolved.And that is why the Cornell case has become larger than a single night at a fraternity house: it now raises questions about how universities investigate sexual assault, how criminal prosecutors assess intoxication and consent, and what accountability should look like when the university's disciplinary process and criminal justice system reach different conclusions.You use AI every day. articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested on treason and espionage allegations
articles.summary: A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor’s office said.
articles.body: A former head of Germany’s foreign intelligence service was arrested on Tuesday on suspicion that he had passed state secrets to a foreign intelligence service, the federal prosecutor’s office said. August Hanning, who led the Federal Intelligence Service, known by its German acronym BND, from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage,” the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement. Hanning, 80, was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. A former aide, identified as Manfred D., was also arrested Tuesday in Steinfurt in western Germany and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage. The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for. The premises of both men were searched Tuesday. Former aide allegedly supplied Hanning with BND documents The prosecutor’s office said Manfred D. worked as Hanning’s chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026. “In his role, he had access to confidential information,” the prosecutor’s office said. Both suspects are believed to have agreed in 2010 to have Manfred D. continuously transmit valuable intelligence from the BND to Hanning in exchange for payment, the statement said. “The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D. provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said. Hanning used the information in private consulting work, and on one occasion “used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D. to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.” Manfred D., who in line with German privacy rules cannot be identified by his full name, provided Hanning with classified information for several years, the statement said, but it was not immediately clear if the collaboration continued until their arrests on Tuesday. The office did not say which country the foreign agent worked for and said “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient.” The statement added that “Hanning was in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D., for several years.” Hanning is suspected of involvement in a prominent child abduction case Hanning came under scrutiny in a separate investigation into the abduction of Hamburg businesswoman Christina Block’s children from her ex-husband in Denmark in January 2024 in a custody battle that had been going on for several years. The investigation into that case led to Tuesday’s arrests. The current proceedings stem from evidence found during a search of Hanning’s residence in connection with that case, the federal prosecutor’s office stated. Hanning and a retired official from the Hamburg State Criminal Police Office are suspected of having accepted a contract from Block in 2022 to abduct her children while serving as executives of a security firm, the public prosecutor’s office announced in the fall of 2025, according to German news agency dpa. The Blocks are a prominent Hamburg family best known for their popular national steakhouse chain Block House. The custody trial has received a lot of attention in the country, with German tabloids offering heavy coverage from the court. A message to the BND for comment was not immediately returned. German opposition lawmaker calls for a quick probe German opposition lawmaker Konstantin von Notz expressed shock about the allegations against Hanning and called for a quick investigation. “This is a hard-hitting and deeply troubling story,” said von Notz, a member of the Greens party and also the German parliament committee overseeing the intelligence services. “We expect a swift and thorough investigation into the egregious allegations leveled against former BND chief Hanning,” von Notz told Spiegel Online. “We have been criticizing the dubious and wide-ranging lobbying activities of former top officials and those with the highest security clearances in the Germany for years,” he said and called for banning former officials with security clearances from engaging in private consulting work after leaving office, Spiegel Online reported.

articles.title: From climbing barricades to Akashvani Bhawan twist: High drama at Rahul-led CEC protest - how it unfolded
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi climbed atop barricades during the INDIA bloc MPs’ march from Parliament towards
articles.body: NEW DELHI: Lok Sabha leader of opposition and Congress MP Rahul Gandhi climbed atop barricades during the INDIA bloc MPs’ march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters in New Delhi on Tuesday, demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation over irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls.Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, NCP-SP MP Supriya Sule and several other opposition leaders also joined the march, which was held amid heavy security and barricading around Parliament and the EC office. Security personnel stopped the march near the NITI Aayog office as the MPs raised slogans of “Vote Chor, Gaddi Chhod”.INDIA bloc MPs stopped near Niti AayogRahul Gandhi led several INDIA bloc MPs in a march from Parliament towards the Election Commission headquarters in New Delhi, with protesters carrying placards and cutouts of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The opposition MPs were demanding Kumar’s removal over alleged irregularities in the Special Intensive Revision (SIR) process.The INDIA bloc had announced the march from Parliament to Nirvachan Sadan as part of its campaign against the Election Commission’s handling of the electoral roll revision. The protest route saw heavy security deployment, with barricades placed across central Delhi and Rapid Action Force personnel deployed around Transport Bhawan ahead of the march.Security personnel stopped the MPs near NITI Aayog, preventing them from proceeding towards the ECI headquarters. Several opposition MPs then sat in protest near Parliament Street.The Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) skipped the march, saying it would pursue the issue through its own means.Opposition leaders detainedLok Sabha Leader of Opposition Rahul Gandhi and other INDIA bloc MPs tried to enter the Election Commission office during their protest march against Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar, but were stopped by security personnel. After being prevented from entering the EC office complex, Congress leaders staged a sit-in outside the premises. The INDIA bloc MPs had marched from Parliament towards Nirvachan Sadan, demanding Kumar’s resignation.Earlier, Rahul Gandhi climbed atop heavy iron barriers near the NITI Aayog office and waved the tricolour while advancing towards the EC headquarters. Tensions escalated as Delhi Police detained Congress MP Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, party General Secretary KC Venugopal and several other INDIA bloc leaders near the NITI Aayog office, where police had barricaded the route to prevent the opposition MPs from reaching Nirvachan Sadan.Rahul, Priyanka Gandhi enter Akashvani Bhawan premises during EC protestRahul Gandhi and Priyanka Gandhi Vadra, along with some other supporters, entered the Akashvani Bhawan premises in an attempt to reach the Election Commission office during the INDIA bloc’s protest demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation.The Congress leaders and other MPs were earlier stopped by security personnel on Parliament Street near the NITI Aayog office while marching towards the EC headquarters. After being prevented from proceeding further, they sat on the road in protest. Rahul Gandhi and TMC MP Abhishek Banerjee later climbed atop a police barricade, while Priyanka Gandhi was taken to a waiting bus for detention.Priyanka Gandhi soon alighted from the bus and joined Rahul Gandhi at the Akashvani gate. Despite being stopped by police, Rahul Gandhi, Priyanka Gandhi and Congress MP Deepender Hooda entered the Akashvani Bhawan premises through the reception gate and were later seen sitting under a tree.Security tightened around protest routeThe march began amid heavy security deployment and barricading in and around Parliament and the Election Commission headquarters. Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Sanjay Raut questioned the security arrangements, saying the MPs intended to proceed peacefully. He also alleged that the CEC had “no moral right” to continue in office, while CPI leader P Sandosh Kumar called him a “Cheating Election Commissioner”.Kharge, Akhilesh target EC over SIR as INDIA bloc MPs press for poll reformsCongress president Mallikarjun Kharge alleged that the Modi government was trying to take away the public’s right to vote and accused Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar of acting at the government’s direction. “After independence, the public was given the right to vote, which the Modi government is trying to end. CEC Gyanesh Kumar is the government's puppet. Gyanesh Kumar does exactly what Modi and Shah say. This will end democracy and the Constitution, and establish dictatorship. The INDIA alliance is fighting against this injustice. We will continue to fight and we will win,” Kharge said.On the INDIA bloc MPs’ protest march, Shiv Sena (UBT) MP Arvind Sawant said, “We want Gyanesh Kumar to be removed, elections to be held on ballot papers, and thirdly, all the people whose names were struck off in the SIR here should be reinstated.” Sawant also alleged, “The Bharatiya Janata Party has a direct connection with the Election Commission.”Samajwadi Party president Akhilesh Yadav also raised the issue, according to the statement shared from Delhi.Opposition steps up attack over SIRThe protest is part of the opposition’s sustained campaign against the SIR exercise and its demand for greater transparency from the poll panel. Congress MP Dharamveer Gandhi alleged that 13 crore votes had been deleted and called it the “biggest fraud in Indian political history”. Congress MP Imran Masood accused Kumar of eroding public trust in the Election Commission, while CPI MP P Sandosh Kumar said the Supreme Court’s observations had strengthened the opposition’s objections to the additional declaration attached to Form 6.“The main demands are crystal clear. Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must go; he should resign. The SIR (Special Intensive Revision) should be scrapped. All the voters who have been removed or deleted under SIR must be restored back onto the voter list,” Congress Rajya Sabha MP Syed Naseer Hussain told ANI. He also demanded a high-level inquiry into alleged political interference in the election machinery.Form 6 row fuels political clashThe march comes a day after the Supreme Court said it had not approved any modified version of Form 6 and said it would examine the Election Commission’s records to determine whether changes had been made and who had authorised them. The EC had earlier said the declaration attached to Form 6 for SIR had been upheld by the Supreme Court and that the forms prescribed under the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, would be used outside the SIR period.Senior Congress leader P Chidambaram said, “How can the BJP blatantly deny that the Chief Justice of India did not say that... he said it clearly, 'we have not approved any modifications to Form 6.' I have seen the declaration... the declaration is indeed a modification of Form 6.”Rahul Gandhi had accused the CEC of changing the application used by citizens to register as new electors “illegally and unilaterally”. BJP national spokesperson Sambit Patra, however, accused Gandhi of misleading the public, saying the Supreme Court had not declared Form 6 illegal and had only agreed to examine allegations concerning changes to the form. The Election Commission has rejected allegations of differences within the three-member poll panel and maintained that decisions relating to SIR were taken unanimously.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: Fox News Digital investigates nightlife in Oxford, Mississippi, where students and local bartenders reveal how easy it is to exploit bar entry policies and bypass security checks.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX: OXFORD, Miss. – "It's rampant for sure." That is how Reagan Fiser, a local bartender who has worked in Oxford nightlife for nearly seven years, describes the sheer volume of underage Ole Miss students slipping into bars around "The Square." It's a bustling college town watering hole hub packed with historic storefronts, crowded balconies and high-volume drinking establishments just a mile away from the University of Mississippi's campus. An extensive investigation by Fox News Digital, backed by interviews with more than 30 students, bartenders and venue employees, reveals an environment where underage drinking thrives around The Square, with students and nightlife workers describing fake IDs, ID sharing and other low-tech methods used to skirt age restrictions. OXFORD MAYOR WARNS KRATOM IS 'ROLLING THE DICE ON DEATH' AS FEARS LINGER OVER OLE MISS DEATHS Oxford Mayor Robyn Tannehill and Police Chief Jeff McCutchen, responding to Fox News Digital's reporting, said the city takes underage drinking, fraudulent identification, illegal drug use and the safety of students, residents and visitors seriously. "We are not suggesting that underage drinking, fake identification, illegal drugs or other safety concerns do not exist in Oxford. Our own enforcement numbers demonstrate that these challenges are real," Tannehill said in a joint statement with McCutchen. Those numbers include 759 false identification cards confiscated, 378 alcohol-possession-by-a-minor violations and 98 fake-ID citations during the calendar-year reporting period, according to Oxford Police. PART I: PREVALENCE & LOOPHOLES 'EVERY STUDENT, EVERY BAR': Underage drinking grips 'The Square' Underage drinking in Oxford is neither hidden nor isolated. One sophomore student verified that getting a fake ID comes down to basic word-of-mouth networking, emphasizing that the culture spans the entire campus: "I think it's everyone, it's everyone ... like every student, no matter if you're in a sorority or fraternity." POLICE NEAR OLE MISS RESPOND TO SUSPECTED OVERDOSE, SAY 'NOT STUDENT-RELATED' "Depending on what year you are, depends on what bar you go to," another female freshman explained. Fiser identified certain bars as "upperclassmen bars" catering to older crowds, while venues operating under Mississippi's 18-plus model serve as magnets for younger students, she said. THE FRAT OMERTÀ: WHISTLEBLOWER WARNS OF ‘CODE OF SILENCE’ AFTER OLE MISS DEATHS, ALLEGED PENN STATE COKE RING While venues mark minors with stamps and patrons older than 21 with wristbands, industry insiders said enforcement collapses in crowded rooms. One bartender mentioned an establishment that serves under-21 crowds "all the time." Fiser added that cheap drink promotions at 18-plus venues create a volatile mix: "Their whole concept is like cheap drinks ... That feels a little sticky." 'PASSING AROUND THE SAME FAKE': Bouncers battle ID sharing Getting past door security rarely requires complex methods; patrons routinely rely on simple hand-offs and ID sharing in line. "I've heard stories of people passing around the same fake, just ... back to the person behind them, and it's working because people don't pay attention," Fiser told Fox News Digital. "And a lot of people don't [try to hide it] because they know they'll get away with it." Local bouncer Haj Bah confirmed catching ID-sharers in real time outside the bar where he works, denying entry to three underage patrons Friday evening — including a pair caught sharing an ID in line.It all happened just moments before his interview with Fox News Digital. VAPE STORE CLERKS NEAR OLE MISS CAMPUS JAILED, FACING DRUG CHARGES A security officer outside flagged a patron handing an ID to another person waiting behind him. "As soon as they came up, I said, 'No.' And for that person who passed the ID over, we asked that person to leave too," Bah said. He went on to say, "Giving that fake ID is the same as a bartender giving alcohol to the child. In my eyes, that is the same thing." While bouncers work to intercept hand-offs, freshman student Drew Ferra noted "how easy" it can be to get served under 21, but argued that venue owners shouldn't bear full blame when patrons present "fakes." "You’re presenting them something that proves you’re 21. In my opinion, should you do it? No. It’s gonna happen though, right?" articles.title: Fastest-growing Ebola outbreak: Kenya confirms first case as citizen who arrived from Congo dies
articles.summary: Kenya on Tuesday confirmed its first case linked to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Africa, the fastest-spreading in history, with a Kenyan citizen who
articles.body: Kenya on Tuesday confirmed its first case linked to the ongoing Ebola outbreak in Africa, the fastest-spreading in history, with a Kenyan citizen who arrived from Congo via Uganda testing positive for the infection.According to Kenyan health minister Aden Duale, the patient arrived in the country on October 3 and had been isolated and treated at a hospital in the capital, Nairobi.The person tested positive for the Ebola virus after developing symptoms associated with hemorrhagic fever and died late Monday while receiving treatment.“Twenty-eight contacts, including family members and health workers who cared for the patient, have been identified. Another 23 passengers who travelled on the same flight from Uganda are being traced,” Duale told reporters.Kenya's health ministry director Patrick Amoth said the contacts will remain in isolation for 21 days. “They will be released after testing negative for Ebola,” he added.The patient will be buried within 24 hours in accordance with recommended public safety protocols.Health authorities have placed Kenya on high alert and are monitoring for possible additional cases.Kenya is the fourth country to record an Ebola case in the current outbreak, which was declared in eastern Congo in May. Uganda recorded 20 cases and France one. Before Kenya reported its case, there had been no active cases outside Congo since Uganda declared its outbreak over in late August.The World Health Organization has warned that the outbreak could become the “deadliest” as it continues to outpace efforts to track and contain it.The outbreak is caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus, for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment. Vaccine and treatment trials are underway in Congo’s Ituri province, the outbreak’s epicenter.(With AP inputs)You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. Take the AIQ test.

articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested for espionage and treason
articles.summary: August Hanning is accused of obtaining classified information for a foreign power.
articles.body:
Former German spy chief August Hanning has been arrested on suspicion of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.

Hanning headed the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.

Prosecutors allege that he used classified intelligence to "draft an analysis" for one foreign intelligence service and maintained contact with another foreign spying service. Investigators have not disclosed which foreign powers were involved.

Police also arrested former BND employee Manfred D, accusing him of passing Hanning about 2,000 classified documents for money.

Manfred D, who was Hanning's bureau chief and remained in the BND until this year, is charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

Local media reported Hanning was arrested at his home in Nordwalde near Münster while Manfred D was arrested in Bavaria. Hanning is due in court on Wednesday and Manfred D will appear on Tuesday.

Prosecutors say Manfred D, who also served as the chief of staff for Hanning's successors between 2012 and 2026, used his role to gain access to highly confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning "in exchange for remuneration".

"The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the Federal Intelligence Service for internal purposes," the statement says.

"On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence ... to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service," prosecutors said, noting it was not clear if "the material reached the intended recipient".

Hanning is also accused of being "in close contact with a representative of another foreign intelligence service, to whom he passed on political information, partially based on material provided by Manfred D, for several years".

Local media say Hanning's alleged possession of intelligence documents came to light during a separate case relating to German steakhouse heiress Christina Block.

Hamburg public prosecutor's office accused Block of orchestrating the kidnapping of her two youngest children in 2023 due to a custody dispute. Investigators allege Hanning was involved in an earlier attempted kidnapping of the children, which he denies.

State criminal police officers reportedly discovered an electronic data storage device containing sensitive information including recent BND documents.

It is not the first time the BND has faced similar controversy. A high-ranking German intelligence officer was charged with treason in 2023 for allegedly passing state secrets to Russia.

Prosecutors alleged Carsten L shared intelligence about the war in Ukraine and the Wagner mercenary group and received roughly €400,000 ($450,000; £340,000). His trial is ongoing.
