articles.title: Fort Hood shooter to be executed by firing squad: All to know
articles.summary: The US Army is averse to capital punishment and has not carried out an execution in decades.
articles.body:
United States President Donald Trump has approved the death by firing squad of Nidal Malik Hasan, a former army officer convicted of carrying out a 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood, an army base in Texas.

The move, if it proceeds, will revive executions in the army, which has not carried one out since 1961.

Death sentences, as well as executions in the US military, are rare and require presidential approval.

Under the army’s code of military justice, premeditated murder does carry the death penalty, but the process is often strict and prolonged.

However, the Trump administration has shown more willingness to seek death penalties for serious crimes, including against civilians.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had initially recommended an execution order for Hasan, and Trump has now approved it, according to an X statement posted by Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell.

Parnell said the time and date of the execution will be set by Army Secretary Adam Telle, who is serving in an acting capacity.

“Judgement day for Hasan has finally come,” he wrote.

On November 5, 2009, the US-born army major, Hasan, a psychiatrist in the force, walked into an army processing centre in Fort Hood, shouted “Allahu Akbar” (God is great) and opened fire on fellow staff members waiting to get medical attention.

Thirteen people were killed, including a pregnant soldier, and 32 others were wounded during 10 minutes of shooting. Analysts have called it the worst shooting at a US military base targeting members of armed forces.

Hasan was shot several times after two officers engaged him and remains paralysed from the waist down.

Hasan was immediately court-martialled, and military prosecutors, from the start, sought the death penalty against him.

However, the process would play out over the course of several years even after his conviction – largely because the US military is averse to capital punishment.

During the trial, Hasan represented himself and admitted to the attacks, saying he was trying to stop deployments to Afghanistan and the killing of his fellow Muslims. He was due to be deployed weeks later.

Investigations revealed Hasan had exchanged emails with Yemeni-American scholar Anwar al-Awlaki, accused of ties to al-Qaeda, before the shooting. He had also repeatedly voiced opposition to the US wars in Iraq and Afghanistan to colleagues and the treatment of Muslims in the army.

Hasan made little effort to defend himself, and his assigned lawyers claimed his testimony aided the opposing side.

He was charged and convicted on 13 counts of premeditated murder in 2013, and jurors recommended the maximum sentence of death. Controversially, Hasan was charged with “workplace violence” because the military justice code does not address the crime of “terrorism”.

The judgement was further delayed by appeals mandated by the military, not because Hasan sought them.

In 2020, the US Army Court of Criminal Appeals upheld the death penalty for Hasan, and in 2023, the US Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces did the same. In March 2025, the US Supreme Court denied a mandatory petition for a judicial review.

In September 2025, Hegseth announced he was seeking presidential approval for Hasan’s execution.

At the time, there was no report of Hegseth specifically seeking death by firing squad.

The president holds the ultimate authority to specify the designated method of execution.

Other forms of execution could have been lethal injection or hanging, which the US military has used in the past.

While Trump’s approval will begin a series of steps towards preparing for the execution, Hasan can still put the process on hold for years with an appeal in the civilian federal court system.

However, that might be unlikely as Hasan made no effort to defend himself during the trial.

He has been remanded to the US Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas, where three other men have also been on the military death row for years.

Among them is Hasan Akbar, convicted of two counts of murder after attacking fellow army members on a Kuwait base in 2003, during the invasion of Iraq.

Another is the convicted serial killer and rapist Ronald Gray, who was found guilty of four counts of murder and eight counts of rape in 2008. He was approved for execution in the same year under President George W Bush, but the process was put on hold by a judge.

Timothy Hennis, a former sergeant, was convicted in 2010 of a triple murder and is also on death row.

The last military execution took place in 1961, when former soldier John Bennett was hanged for the rape of an 11-year-old girl.

articles.title: Burning cars, clashes and mass arrests: France’s student protests spread across the country - videos
articles.summary: High-school students across France blockaded hundreds of schools on Tuesday as a weeks-old nationwide protest over school funding, overcrowded classrooms
articles.body: High-school students across France blockaded hundreds of schools on Tuesday as a weeks-old nationwide protest over school funding, overcrowded classrooms and poor infrastructure showed no sign of easing. Injuries and clashes with police intensified amid pressure on the government.The demonstrations, which began in the Paris region in mid-September and spread to cities and towns across France, have led to widespread school closures, arrests and confrontations between teenage protesters and police.The French government said 215 students and 715 police officers had been injured since the protests began. France's Justice Ministry said 5,060 people have been arrested since the protests began, with 87 per cent of them minors. More than 1,800 people are being prosecuted, including 1,483 minors, the ministry said, without specifying the crimes. It said 790 cases had been dismissed.Police have used tear gas and riot-control weapons to disperse demonstrators, with authorities describing some of the unrest as "urban violence". Unions, rights groups and students have accused police of using disproportionate force.Interior minister Laurent Nunez said late Monday that police had opened 10 internal investigations into allegations of brutality since the protests began.The protests escalated after two serious injuries involving students. In Lens, in northern France, a 15-year-old boy lost his hand during a confrontation on Monday.In Paris, hooded youths set fire to the entrance of a high school on Monday, while footage from the demonstrations showed burning cars, people running through streets and clashes with police.Parents, union activists and other adults gathered at the school wearing white armbands, with local media reporting that their "aim of creating a buffer zone" was to keep teenage protesters and police apart.Students said their grievances include run-down classrooms, shortages of desks and chairs, insufficient teachers, exhausting workloads and schools that become extremely hot during summer. articles.title: JIMMY FAILLA: I came to Fox with my taxi double-parked. Then came the ride of my life
articles.summary: Comedian and host Jimmy Failla reflects on Fox News Channel's 30th anniversary, sharing how the former NYC cab driver fell in love with the energy at "1211," aka Fox News headquarters.
articles.body: I'd like to start by congratulating all of my incredible colleagues at Fox News on this huge anniversary. And let the record show that our channel may be turning 30, but it only looks 22 thanks to the makeup team. Like a lot of people who work here at Fox, I absolutely fell in love with the energy in the building the very first time I walked in the door. The only difference was that I couldn't stay long, because I had my taxi double-parked on Sixth Avenue, and I didn't want to get a parking ticket. JIMMY FAILLA RECALLS DOUBLE-PARKING CAB ON 6TH AVENUE TO SQUEEZE IN FIRST FOX TV APPEARANCE As you may have heard, I was a New York City cab driver the first time I appeared on Fox, but let the record show that this place has taken me on the ride of my life since then. That being said, I'm not here to make this piece about me or my nationally syndicated talk show, which you can listen to weekdays from noon-3 p.m. on the Fox News app. Nor do I want to focus on my TV show, "Fox News Saturday Night with Jimmy Failla," which airs at 10 p.m. ET on the Fox News Channel. Don't get me wrong, a more shameless writer might even use this opportunity to plug his New York Times bestselling book, "Cancel Culture Dictionary," but let's leave my accolades aside — especially my top streaming stand-up comedy special, "They're Just Jokes," which is streaming on Fox Nation. Getting past my ridiculousness for a minute, the thing that makes so many people fall in love with working here is the undeniable sense of community that energizes "1211" every day. MARTHA MACCALLUM: AFTER 22 YEARS, HERE'S WHY I'M GRATEFUL TO CALL FOX HOME Everybody knows EVERYBODY, and as serious as the work can get, the day-to-day vibe feels more like you're hanging out with your funniest friends. Sure, people put in crazy hours and work against tight deadlines, but we spend every second in between cracking each other up during commercial breaks and catching up on each other's families. As serious as the work can get, the day-to-day vibe feels more like you're hanging out with your funniest friends. JENNIFER GRIFFIN: I COVERED WARS, TERROR AND TRAGEDY FOR FOX NEWS. WHAT I FOUND WAS A FAMILY Those conversations frequently make their way to the airwaves, which is why the viewers know so much about our pets, our kids and our weekend plans. In every sense of the word, Fox News is a family, on-air and off, which is why we have so many families watching us at home. FOX NEWS MEDIA'S SPOTLIGHT AWARDS CELEBRATE BEHIND-THE-SCENES STARS AS NETWORK NEARS 30 YEARS I'm always told at my live events that people feel like they know us because they DO. We're like relatives, and the best part is you never have to worry about us staying too long because you have a remote that makes us leave. (Although we may ask to borrow money before we go if I lose my bet on the Yankees winning the World Series this year.) LAUREN GREEN: I WAS FOX NEWS CHANNEL'S FIRST ON-AIR HIRE. HERE'S HOW A DREAM BECAME A POWERHOUSE The other thing that makes our channel so dominant on so many platforms is the fact that TV is the ultimate team game, and it's not lost on any of us that NOBODY can win on the air without superstar performances off it. Tom Brady wouldn't have a single Super Bowl ring if he didn't have a great offensive line, and the same goes for TV hosts — we're nothing without all the amazing people blocking for us behind the scenes. DANA PERINO: THE UNTOLD STORY OF THE REMARKABLE PEOPLE WHO MAKE FOX NEWS POSSIBLE Not that I think anyone should be comparing themselves to a man of Tom Brady's stature, but it wouldn't shock me if Jesse Watters did. Happy 30th anniversary to ALL of Fox News. From the wizards in the wardrobe department to the badasses in building operations and everyone in between. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP There are honestly too many awesome people here to name, although I do hope this piece has inspired at least half of you to start watching my show because I can always use the ratings. Cheers to 30 years! CLICK HERE FOR MORE FROM JIMMY FAILLA

articles.body: Republicans funnel hundreds of millions of dollars into midterm races. Text messages show how Cornell fraternity brothers sought to coordinate their responses after rape allegations came to light. And televangelist Jim Bakker dies at 86. Here’s what to know today. Republicans fight midterm chaos with influx of late money Republicans have made more than $700 million worth of new advertising bookings in congressional races since the start of September, according to an NBC News analysis of data from AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm. By comparison, Democrats booked more than $430 million in new ad reservations across those races last month. This is Morning Rundown, a weekday newsletter to start your day. Sign up here to get it in your inbox. The unprecedented flood of late ad spending in House and Senate races will test whether hundreds of millions of dollars can buy the GOP some reprieve as it combats eroding standing among voters. In the battle for the Senate majority, almost 7 of every 10 newly booked advertising dollars are coming from Republicans. The party has poured almost $150 million in new ad dollars to back Ken Paxton over Democrat James Talarico. In the House, a bit less than 6 in 10 new ad dollars are coming from the GOP. Take a closer look at which races account for the most spending. For subscribers: Many Latino voters across Texas are feeling buyer’s remorse when it comes to voting for Donald Trump in 2024. Here’s what they had to say. For subscribers: The DOJ is moving to revoke the citizenship of 40 foreign-born Americans, marking the largest effort in recent history to denaturalize U.S. citizens. The Supreme Court’s new term began with justices seemingly stumped by a case that seeks to hold Exxon Mobil and Suncor Energy liable for the impacts of climate change. Baltic countries prep for a potential Russian invasion In recent months, several Baltic nations have seen a growing number of Russian incursions into their airspace, as the Kremlin tests the limits of its neighbors. Lithuania, nestled between Kremlin-allied Belarus and the Russian enclave of Kaliningrad, fears they’re at the top of the target list. That’s why the government-backed paramilitary organization, the Lithuanian Riflemen’s Union, has seen a boom in new volunteers since Russia’s 2022 invasion of Ukraine, with 18,000 registered as of 2025. About a third are “junior riflemen” aged 11 to 18. But Baltic countries are not anticipating a repeat of scenes from the Kremlin’s full-scale invasion, when Russian tanks rolled into Ukraine. Instead, they’re bracing for a hybrid approach that includes cyberattacks, disinformation, sabotage and drones while Russia maintains a degree of deniability. Read more of Richard Engel’s reporting inside Lithuania. Texts show how Cornell frat brothers reacted to rape allegations When two of the Chi Phi brothers since accused of sexually assaulting Jane Doe first learned in a text message chat that Cornell University had suspended the fraternity, one responded to the chapter’s then-president with a single word: “F--k.” As news spread across campus that a student alleged that she was raped and plied with drugs at a fraternity party in October 2024, Chi Phi members expressed worry and tried to get their stories straight, according to text messages, campus police and university disciplinary records obtained by NBC News. The man who replied with profanity immediately asked whether he should call Doe but was told to wait. Televangelist Jim Bakker dies at 86 Jim Bakker, the charismatic evangelical preacher who built a Christian television empire, only to see it collapse in scandal, recrimination and prison, has died at the age of 86, his wife, Lori, announced. Bakker and his first wife, Tammy Faye, gained popularity in the 1970s after starting a TV puppet show, and later a high-energy talk show called “The PTL Club.” Bakker also launched the first Christian satellite network and built a multimillion-dollar empire complete with one of the world’s largest theme parks, Heritage USA, on the small donations of hundreds of thousands of believers, some of whom pledged their life savings. But PTL collapsed after reports of a $250,000 payment and lavish spending came to light. More on Bakker’s life and legacy. L.C., the landmark Supreme Court ruling that helped disabled people receive care in their communities rather than institutions. My colleague Colleen Long and I set out to understand what drove such a sweeping reversal and what it could mean for millions of Americans. The answer led us to Trump’s crackdown on homelessness. After the president demanded action against tent encampments in American cities, his administration began pushing to make it easier to force homeless people with serious mental illness into treatment. That agenda eventually collided with federal disability policy, prompting Stephen Miller to press the DOJ to reconsider its approach to Olmstead, according to people familiar with the internal discussions. Not everyone was caught by surprise. Two days before the DOJ released its opinion, a White House aide from Miller’s office previewed the change during a previously undisclosed meeting with activists and conservative think tank leaders whom the administration hoped would publicly support it. articles.title: Russia plague quarantine following lab death: Should we be worried?
articles.summary: Plague is still endemic to Siberia, the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak.
articles.body:
Dozens of people have been quarantined in Russia’s Siberia after a laboratory worker at a plague research institute fell ill and died in undisclosed circumstances.

Russian news outlet People of Baikal reported the woman may have contracted pneumonic plague from a broken test tube and died.

Plague is a severe, life-threatening infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis. Between 1346 and 1353, the bubonic plague – one of three forms of the disease – was known as the Black Death. It caused one of the most fatal pandemics in the world across Eurasia and North Africa. Some 30-60 percent of the population of Europe is believed to have died in that outbreak.

Pneumonic plague is less common than bubonic plague. It is a severe form of the infection that can spread from person to person.

What happened in the Russian lab and should we be worried?

On Monday, Russian media reported that a 28-year-old woman named Darya Shipilova, who had been working at the Irkutsk Anti-plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died from suspected pneumonic plague last week.

According to Russian media reports, Shipilova became ill while at work on September 30 and died two days later at a hospital in the nearby town of Shelekhov. Several media reports suggest there may have been an accident at the lab, but this has not been officially confirmed.

About 200 people who came into contact with the dead woman have since been quarantined, and parts of the hospital where she died have also been cordoned off. An aluminium plant nearby has instructed its workers to wear masks.

Anna Popova, head of Russia’s public health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, flew to Irkutsk to meet with Governor Igor Kobzev and other officials four days ago.

In a statement quoted by the TASS news agency, Rospotrebnadzor said officials in the Irkutsk region had detected two cases ⁠of COVID and two cases of rhinoviruses among people who had been in contact with the researcher. No other cases of infectious diseases were noted.

Later on Monday, Russian authorities said they found no evidence that the woman’s illness was caused by any of the pathogens she worked with and said the situation was under control.

Kobzev said in ⁠a statement that the woman had died of “pneumonia of unknown aetiology”, adding: “Importantly, over the past few days, no new cases of staff from the Anti-Plague Institute seeking medical attention have been identified.”

He added that the situation was under control and that all known contacts with the dead woman had been identified, examined and placed under medical supervision.

What is plague and what are its symptoms?

The bacterium which causes plague, Yersinia pestis, is carried by small wild mammals and their fleas. In Siberia, where it is endemic, it is rare for Russians to fall ill with the plague, however. But cases occur every year in other parts of the world, notably in Africa.

According to the Centres for Disease Control (CDC) in the US, plague has been detected in people of all ages, from babies to those aged in their 90s. Half of the cases occur in people aged 12 to 45. Men and women are susceptible, although it has been slightly more common among men.

There are three main types of plague, affecting different parts of the body. These are bubonic, septicaemic and pneumonic . According to the World Health Organization (WHO), bubonic plague is the most common clinical form. Symptoms include painful swollen lymph nodes or “buboes”.

Septicaemic plague infects the blood while pneumonic plague affects the lungs.

The WHO describes septicaemic and pneumonic plague as “less common, but severe forms” of plague.

A fourth type, pharyngeal plague, is rare. It can be contracted by eating infected meat.

According to the US-based Cleveland Clinic, besides swollen lymph nodes in the case of bubonic plague, those infected with any of the forms of plague can display the following symptoms:

Specific symptoms for Septicaemic plague, which can occur as a complication of bubonic plague, include abdominal pain and blackness in tissues, particularly on figures, toes and the nose, according to the CDC.

Pneumonic plague, which occurs when bacteria from bubonic or septicaemic infections reach the lungs, is accompanied by shortness of breath, chest pain, coughing and sometimes bloody mucus.

Other complications can also arise from plague if it is untreated, according to the Cleveland Clinic. These include:

Meningitis – a severe infection that causes inflammation of the lining of the brain and spinal cord.

Tissue death and loss of limbs from gangrene.

Bubonic plague has a death rate of 30 to 60 percent. Pneumonic and septicaemic plague are fatal if left untreated within one to six days, the WHO says.

If identified quickly, however, all forms can be treated with antibiotics.

Plague most commonly spreads through the bites of fleas carried by rodents, but can also be transmitted from person to person.

According to the CDC in the US, people can also become infected through exposure to sick pets, especially cats.

These are the main ways the disease can be transmitted:

According to the CDC, people and animals can contract plague from dead rats carrying the disease, as well as being bitten by fleas that have bitten infected rats. “Dogs and cats may also bring plague-infected fleas into the home. Flea bite exposure may result in primary bubonic plague or septicemic plague,” the CDC states.

Humans can contract plague through contact with the tissue or body fluids of an infected animal. This form of exposure most commonly results in bubonic plague or septicaemic plague, according to the CDC.

Droplets coughed out by humans and animals infected with pneumonic plague can hang in the air and be inhaled by another person. The CDC states that this requires direct and close contact with the person or animal with pneumonic plague, and it is the only way the disease can be transmitted from person to person.

According to the CDC, the last documented case of person-to-person pneumonic plague transmission was in 1924. However, there have been more recent cases of pneumonic plague transmitted to humans by sick cats.

“Cats are particularly susceptible to plague and can be infected by eating infected rodents. Cats with plague pose a risk of transmitting infectious plague droplets to their owners or to veterinarians,” the CDC states.

Ian Jones, professor of virology at the University of Reading, told The Associated Press news agency that “plague carries a huge history and is still present in many parts of the world, including Russia.”

Worldwide, there are between 1,000 and 2,000 cases of plague every year, according to Cleveland Clinic in the US.

Plague is endemic to Siberia, which is the location of the first known prehistoric human outbreak. Besides Russia, plague is also endemic in several countries, according to the WHO. Between 2019 and 2025, most new cases recorded by the WHO occurred in the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Madagascar.

There have been rare cases elsewhere. In July 2025, an Arizona man who worked with cats died of pneumonic plague – the first such death since 2007.

There was a major outbreak of bubonic plague in Los Angeles in 1924-1925, after it was first recorded in the US in 1900, brought by infected rats on steamships. Bubonic plague has made up 80 percent of an average of seven cases per year in the US since then. Most of these have occurred in northern New Mexico, northern Arizona, southern Colorado, California, southern Oregon and western Nevada, according to the CDC.

Why has this incident triggered global alarm?

While authorities in Russia have stressed that postmortem tests carried out on the woman did not detect that she had plague, the incident has raised global alarm.

Several authorities have called on Russia to give more clarity about what exactly happened to the woman at the lab.

In Washington, United States President Donald Trump said he was watching the situation with concern and that the US would be willing to help, though he said he had not spoken to Russian President Vladimir Putin about the situation.

“It’s a rough disease. You know, that’s a disease we used to be able to control, but somehow those microbes have gotten stronger and smarter. They’re like an army,” Trump told reporters outside the White House.

“Even with great advancement, the germs have really become relatively stronger than they were, and things that used to work on pneumonia don’t work as well any more,” he added.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said on Monday that he does not believe there is cause for alarm, but that the US is watching the case closely, aware that “it could spread quickly” despite the quarantine and other public health protocols.

On Monday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the public and media should follow official statements from Rospotrebnadzor, rather than “rumours or speculation”.

“It is difficult to comment with confidence given the relatively limited information currently available,” Malick Gibani, clinical associate professor in bacterial vaccinology at Imperial College London, said in a statement to the media.

“Based on reports, there appears to be a suspected index case, and contacts have been quarantined. If there is an exposure in a laboratory to a potentially dangerous pathogen, the usual procedure would be to undertake a risk assessment of who may have been exposed and the nature of their contact.”

He added: “People considered at risk can then be monitored and, where appropriate, screening, quarantine, or post-exposure prophylaxis with antibiotics may be offered. I think it’s important that we see how this pans out, and ideally, there’d be good communication between the public health authorities and the wider global health community.

“I think this emphasises the need to be aware of ongoing outbreaks of serious bacterial pathogens and highlights the need for investment in biosecurity, particularly for preventing biological risks. This could include developing medical countermeasures like better diagnostics or vaccines,” Gibani said.

articles.title: US, China in talks for reciprocal visits to nuclear sites in bid to build trust, prevent arms race
articles.summary: The United States has discussed starting reciprocal visits to nuclear sites with China, amid efforts to build mutual trust and prevent an arms race
articles.body: The United States has discussed starting reciprocal visits to nuclear sites with China, amid efforts to build mutual trust and prevent an arms race between the rivals.According to a Tuesday report by CNN, the US plans to continue pushing for that possibility during in-person meetings in the coming months.The talks reportedly proposed visits to the US department of energy national labs and to China’s equivalent facilities.Additionally, the US would be open to discussing visits to nuclear testing sites, a source told CNN.The US is reportedly concerned about China’s rapidly growing nuclear weapons program. Furthermore, the USA's last remaining arms control agreement with Russia expired in 2025.The efforts to establish a trilateral agreement with China and Russia began in President Donald Trump’s initial term, but largely went in vain, with China and Russia largely ignoring the US outreach.Beijing has maintained that its nuclear arsenal is much smaller than those of Russia and the US, and argues that this makes its involvement in such negotiations unnecessary.However, according to CNN, the current idea of reciprocal visits was initially raised by Beijing as an indication of openness to confidence-building measures. The discussions have been at the working level between American and Chinese officials, on the sidelines of gatherings by the five permanent members of the United Nations Security Council.Former acting assistant secretary of state Paul Dean, who oversaw US arms control efforts, told CNN that the administration should enter any nuclear talks with China with its "eyes wide open."He added, however, that reciprocal visits would be "an extremely valuable confidence-building measure" and could build the informational and diplomatic groundwork for further efforts to reduce nuclear risk between the two nations."This is a very dangerous time, and there are very few guardrails in place on the US-China nuclear relationship," said Dean, who is now a vice president at the nonprofit Nuclear Threat Initiative.A further Trump-Xi meeting this year is widely seen as likely, possibly at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China in November or at the Group of 20 meetings in the US in December.According to the official quoted by CNN, lower-level talks on possible nuclear site visits are expected to take place before the two leaders meet again.You use AI every day. articles.title: PCs who used Taser and baton on Donald Burgess at care home sacked
articles.summary: A disciplinary hearing finds both officers used unnecessary force on Donald Burgess at his care home.
articles.body:
Two police officers who pepper-sprayed and Tasered a 92-year-old amputee at a care home have been sacked for gross misconduct.

PC Stephen Smith and PC Rachel Comotto, who were both acquitted of assault occasioning actual bodily harm in May 2025, had been called to Park Beck care home in St Leonards-on-Sea after resident Donald Burgess threatened carers with a dinner knife.

Burgess, who had dementia, was hit with a baton, pepper sprayed and Tasered as he sat in his wheelchair in his bedroom in June 2022.

At Sussex Police headquarters in Lewes on Tuesday, a disciplinary panel decided there had been "unjustified and excessive use of force" and dismissed both officers without notice.

Burgess was taken to hospital after the incident, where he contracted Covid and died 22 days later, but the officers were not held responsible for his death.

The misconduct panel found Comotto and Smith did not attempt to de-escalate the situation before using force and had breached standards of professional behaviour.

Both were also placed on the College of Policing's barred list.

During a week-long hearing, force lawyer Aaron Rathmell told the panel Smith, 52, and Comotto, 37, "acted, hastily, harshly and lost control".

He said Smith had drawn the pepper spray within nine seconds of entering Burgess's room.

Bodyworn camera footage showed Smith walking into the room and saying: "Do you want to be sprayed or Tasered? It's up to you. Can you put that down for us?"

Despite repeated requests, Burgess, who was a single leg amputee, did not drop the dinner knife.

The panel found Smith "made no attempt to assess or understand" Burgess's vulnerability, while Comotto "showed no compassion".

The following video contains distressing scenes.

Smith failed to consider leaving the 92-year-old in his room to calm down, the panel found, plus the use of Pava, a type of pepper spray, was deemed unreasonable in the circumstances.

There was "limited mitigation" for this behaviour, it said.

The panel also said Smith's tone and language towards Burgess was "dismissive in nature", while Comotto was "antagonistic".

Comotto's statements - such as "last chance" or "seriously" - and giving Burgess limited time to respond, were found to be inappropriate.

The panel found her use of force to be unreasonable.

Assistant Chief Constable Peter Gardner said Burgess was in his own room, isolated from residents and posed no risk.

More information should have been ascertained from care home staff, he said.

Gardner added that Smith had shown a lack of remorse and insight into the inappropriateness of his actions, and the panel remained concerned by his evidence which stated he would not do anything differently.

While noting Comotto's remorse and evidence that she would act differently, Gardner said the reputation of the police service, along with public confidence in it, must be upheld.

articles.title: Jim Bakker, 'PTL Club' televangelist and fmr husband of Tammy Faye, dead at 86
articles.summary: Televangelist Jim Bakker, the host of the popular “The PTL Club" TV show with his former wife Tammy Faye Bakker, died Monday at the age of 86.
articles.body: Televangelist Jim Bakker, who rose to fame with the "The PTL Club" TV show before admitting to a sexual encounter with a church clerk and being convicted of financial crimes, has died at the age of 86. Bakker's second wife, Lori, said Jim passed away on Monday. His cause of death is unclear, and it comes after Bakker suffered a stroke in 2020. "It is with a broken heart that I share that my beloved husband, Jim Bakker, went home to be with the Lord this evening," Lori Bakker said in a statement. "For 66 years, Jim gave his life to preaching the Gospel of Jesus Christ. He was a pioneer of Christian television, but to me, he was my husband, my best friend, and the man I was honored to walk beside through so many seasons of life and ministry. "Jim loved people deeply. He loved this ministry, and he loved the friends and partners who stood with him throughout the years. Even in his final days, his heart was still for the work of God and for the Gospel to continue reaching the world," she added. NOAH'S ARK MYSTERY ENTERS NEW PHASE AS RESEARCHERS PROBE DEEP BENEATH SITE Bakker was born in Muskegon, Michigan, and attended North Central Bible College in Minneapolis, where he met his first wife, Tammy Faye. They married in 1961 and dropped out of college to start their own traveling ministry. He preached, while she sang and played the accordion as they crossed the country, visiting churches and tent revivals. "In the 1960s, he joined the Christian Broadcasting Network under the direction of Pat Robertson. Jim developed one of the first daily, one-hour, kids’ shows for Christians called 'Come On Over,'" read a biography of Bakker on his website. "He also later became the first host of a ground-breaking talk show called 'The 700 Club,' featuring many of the top ministers and singers of the day." Bakker then left CBN in 1972 and two years later formed the PTL Satellite Network. "The PTL Club" — with PTL standing for "Praise the Lord" — became its signature show. During the peak of its popularity in the 1980s, "The PTL Club" was drawing millions of viewers and bringing in millions of dollars annually from followers, according to The Associated Press. The show was based around chats with guests and Christian entertainers, with Bakker offering upbeat sermons and Tammy Faye singing. Their ministry also included the Christian-based Heritage USA theme park and hotel in Fort Mill, South Carolina. FULTON SHEEN BECAME A TV SENSATION PREACHING FAITH, MORALITY AND WARNINGS MICHAEL KNOWLES SAYS STILL RESONATE However, Bakker's empire began to unravel in March 1987 when he admitted to a sexual encounter with church clerk Jessica Hahn, forcing him to turn over operations to pastor and broadcaster Jerry Falwell. In 1988, Bakker was indicted for mail fraud, wire fraud and conspiracy after an investigation of PTL’s finances. He was convicted and sentenced to 45 years in federal prison, though the sentence was later reduced to eight years. At a news conference after Bakker was found guilty, Tammy Faye stood in front of the microphones and sang the hymn, "On Christ the Solid Rock I Stand," the AP reported. Tammy Faye then divorced Bakker in 1992 while he was still in prison. She married Roe Messner, a building contractor whose projects included the Heritage USA theme park. Messner spent about two years in prison after being convicted of bankruptcy fraud in 1995, while Tammy Faye later died of colon cancer in 2007. Bakker, meanwhile, was released on parole in 1995 and married Lori in 1998. The couple launched "The Jim Bakker Show" on the PTL Satellite Network five years later. "The Jim Bakker Show is an hour-long daily broadcast featuring prophetic and Biblical revelations brought to light in today’s world. In these end times God is providing answers and wisdom to be revealed at just the right time. And the time is now!" the show says on its website. Bakker and Tammy Faye had two children. He and his second wife adopted five children in 2002. CLICK HERE TO GET THE FOX NEWS APP The Associated Press also reported that in June 2021, Bakker and his Morningside Church Productions Inc. settled a lawsuit accusing him of falsely claiming the health supplement Silver Solution could cure COVID-19. The settlement called for $156,000 in refunds to people who paid money or gave contributions to obtain the product in the early days of the pandemic. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: Egyptian journalists from fact-checking website facing terrorism charges
articles.summary: Matsda2sh rejects the accusation by prosecutors that its entire newsroom belongs to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
articles.body:
Prosecutors in Egypt have charged six journalists working for the independent fact-checking platform Matsda2sh with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood, according to their lawyer.

Nabeh al-Ganadi said on Monday that the men were accused of joining a terrorist group, funding terrorism, publishing "fake news", and using social media to call for acts of terrorism, he added. Matsda2sh has denied the allegations.

Later, Ganadi said the State Security Prosecution had remanded five of them in custody for 15 days, and that the sixth was still being interrogated.

The journalists' arrests last week were condemned by international human rights and press freedom organisations.

The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) called the detention of Matsda2sh's entire newsroom a "grave escalation in Egypt's campaign against independent journalism".

It said the country remained one of the world's leading jailers of journalists, with 25 currently imprisoned or detained.

President Abdul Fattah al-Sisi has overseen what human rights groups say is an unprecedented crackdown on dissent since he led the military's overthrow of his predecessor, Muslim Brotherhood leader Mohammed Morsi, in 2013.

Tens of thousands of people have been detained, mainly Muslim Brotherhood officials and supporters but also leading secular and liberal activists, media workers and academics.

Matsda2sh, whose name means "Do Not Believe" in Arabic, was founded in 2018 to "resist the flow of false or misleading news", according to its website.

It regularly fact-checks statements made by Egyptian officials and carries out investigative reporting in Egypt and other Arab countries.

Security personnel arrested the six Matsda2sh journalists - Abdullah Qadry, Mohammed Ashraf Abu Emeira, Islam Barakat, Omar Helal, Mohammed Mahmoud, and Mohammed Adel - in a series of raids on their homes across Egypt on 28 and 29 September, according to the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), whose lawyers are defending them.

Initially, no information was provided about where they were being held or the reasons for their detention, the EIPR said.

On Thursday, the Egyptian interior ministry confirmed their arrests and accused Matsda2sh of seeking to destabilise the country through disinformation.

It said the platform was unlicensed and operated from abroad, and that its founder, Abdel Rahman Mansour, was member of the Muslim Brotherhood.

In an interview with the CPJ that day, Mansour insisted that the accusations "misrepresent who we are and the work we do".

"We have no affiliation with the Muslim Brotherhood, and the authorities know this," he said.

On Monday, the EIPR said most of the detained journalists had testified before the State Security Prosecution that they were "tortured at National Security Agency facilities in the days following their arrests, before being brought before any judicial authority".

The journalists reported "beatings, forced stripping, electric shocks and threats to harm them or their families", it added.

The interior ministry denied that they had been tortured or mistreated.

A ministry source said the EIPR's allegations were "unfounded and come in the context of attempts to evade the charges levelled at them".

articles.title: A Wisconsin bargain hunter paid just $29 for a flower painting at a rummage sale; about a decade later it was authenticated as a Martin Johnson Heade and sold at Christie’s for $882,500
articles.summary: A Wisconsin bargain hunter paid just $29 for a flower painting at a rummage sale, with no idea that the artwork would eventually be worth a fortune.
articles.body: A Wisconsin bargain hunter paid just $29 for a flower painting at a rummage sale, with no idea that the artwork would eventually be worth a fortune. About a decade later, the painting was identified as a work by American artist Martin Johnson Heade and went on to Christie’s in New York. According to Christie’s auction record, Two Magnolias on Blue Plush sold for $882,500 on May 26, 1999, after carrying an estimate of $300,000 to $500,000. The sale turned an inexpensive rummage-sale purchase into one of the more remarkable art discoveries of its time.A $29 painting with a surprising historyThe painting began its journey to the auction block in an unlikely place: a Wisconsin rummage sale. A man from Wausau bought the artwork for just $29 because he liked the way the magnolia flowers were depicted. At the time, there was little indication that the painting was the work of a notable 19th-century American artist.It stayed with the buyer for roughly a decade before experts recognised its significance. The work was identified as Two Magnolias on Blue Plush, a floral still life by Martin Johnson Heade, who lived from 1819 to 1904. What had initially looked like an inexpensive decorative painting was now considered an important work by an established American artist.Christie’s confirms the Heade attributionChristie’s official catalogue identifies the artist as Martin Johnson Heade and the work as Two Magnolias on Blue Plush. It is an oil painting on canvas measuring 15 by 24 inches. The auction house records the work as signed by Heade, although the signature is described as indistinct. Christie’s also provides extensive background on Heade’s magnolia paintings and their importance within his career.The painting was offered in Christie’s Important American Paintings, Drawings & Sculpture sale in New York on May 26, 1999. Its estimated price was between $300,000 and $500,000. Instead, bidding pushed the final price to $882,500. That result transformed the story of the Wisconsin rummage-sale purchase into an extraordinary art-market bargain. A painting bought for $29 had eventually sold for hundreds of thousands of dollars.Why Heade's magnolia paintings were importantThe value of the painting was not simply a result of its unusual discovery story. Much of its importance came from Heade himself and the distinctive way he approached floral subjects. Heade worked in several genres, including landscapes and still lifes, but his magnolia paintings became particularly notable. Christie’s describes the magnolia series as the culmination of his career and among his most original American still-life works. His treatment of the flowers was different from a conventional floral arrangement. Instead of placing magnolias upright in a vase, Heade frequently showed the blossoms lying across richly coloured fabric.In Two Magnolias on Blue Plush, the pale flowers are set against blue velvet, creating a sharp contrast between the blossoms and the dark, luxurious background. Christie’s notes that Heade paid close attention to the individual flower, exploring its form, texture and delicate details. The magnolia became more than simply a decorative subject; it was the central focus of the composition.From overlooked artwork to auction treasureThe painting's discovery was especially striking because it had not been purchased from a gallery or recognised as an important artwork when it changed hands. The Wausau buyer found it in an ordinary rummage-sale setting and paid a modest amount for it. It was only later, after examination and identification, that the painting's connection to Heade became clear. The story became part of a wider fascination with valuable American artworks turning up in unlikely places.A remarkable difference in valueThe numbers alone show how dramatic the transformation was. The original purchase price was $29. Christie’s estimated the painting at $300,000 to $500,000 before the auction. It ultimately sold for $882,500. The auction price was therefore more than 30,000 times the amount originally paid for the painting.But the price was driven by more than the bargain behind its discovery. The painting had the artistic importance, provenance and attribution necessary to make it valuable in the serious American art market. Christie’s describes Heade’s magnolia paintings as an important part of his artistic legacy, helping explain why Two Magnolias on Blue Plush attracted such strong interest at auction.The wider fascination with Heade's lost treasuresThe Wisconsin discovery was not the only story involving Heade paintings being found outside the traditional art market. Later reporting by TIME described several Heade flower paintings that had been purchased for surprisingly small amounts at garage and estate sales before being recognised and sold for much larger sums. The stories added to the appeal of Heade's work and demonstrated how artworks can sometimes remain unidentified for years. At the same time, the market for Heade paintings also faced concerns about authenticity.From $29 to $882,500 The story of Two Magnolias on Blue Plush is ultimately about a remarkable change in perspective. What one Wisconsin buyer saw as an attractive flower painting at a rummage sale eventually emerged as a work attributed to an important American artist. Christie’s sold Martin Johnson Heade’s painting for $882,500 in 1999, turning a $29 purchase into an extraordinary art-world discovery. The sale remains a striking example of how an overlooked artwork can acquire an entirely different value once its history and artist are properly recognised.You use AI every day. articles.title: Ukraine launches major drone attack on Russia’s Moscow region, killing two
articles.summary: Russia says 290 drones targeted Moscow and nearby regions in the overnight Ukrainian assault.
articles.body:
Ukraine has launched a major drone attack on Moscow, killing two people and setting fire to a warehouse in the capital city, Russian officials say.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said on Tuesday that the overnight assault involved 650 drones heading towards the city, most of which were shot down, as both sides intensify long-range strikes on infrastructure before winter.

Regional Governor Andrei Vorobyov said one person was killed in Radumlya and another was killed in Barbybino. He said seven people had been injured and that 47 houses, four apartments and three cars had been damaged.

He said 185 drones were “destroyed or neutralised” over the wider region.

Prominent war blogger Yuri Podolyaka said an oil storage tank was hit at the Volodarskaya oil storage and distribution facility, the biggest in the Moscow region. The facility stores diesel, petrol and jet fuel. There was no official confirmation that it had been hit.

Volodarskaya is one of the major hubs in the distribution system of Transneft and is linked to Moscow’s main oil refinery. It supplies fuel to all three of the capital’s large airports.

Ukraine has increasingly targeted oil refineries, depots and export terminals in ⁠an effort to deprive Moscow of the revenues it needs to ⁠finance the war that Russia began in February 2022.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Dmitry Medvenko said the attack ended a relative lull in large Ukrainian strikes on Moscow since September 20.

Separately on Tuesday, a Ukrainian drone attack on a minibus in the Russian-occupied part of the Ukrainian Zaporizhia region killed three people, Moscow-installed authorities said.

Russia has recently intensified ⁠attacks on the Ukrainian capital, Kyiv, sending waves of missiles and drones by night and day. Its latest targets have included bridges across the Dnipro River.

Kremlin-appointed official Yevgeny Balitsky said on Telegram that a Ukrainian drone hit the minibus close to a village near the front line, killing “three people, including the driver” and wounding three passengers.

Both Russia and Ukraine have increased strikes in the fifth year of the war, with diplomacy so far failing to end fighting and the United Nations warning of a significant rise in civilian deaths.

articles.title: James Carville warns Dems against impeaching Trump if they win control in midterms
articles.summary: James Carville warned the Supreme Court shields Trump from consequences while Al Hunt calls impeachment a "waste of energy" that won't succeed.
articles.body: Veteran Democratic strategist James Carville urged Democrats to avoid pursuing a third impeachment of President Donald Trump if the party wins control of the House of Representatives in November, arguing it would be "highly unlikely" to succeed. On the "Politics War Room" podcast on Thursday, Carville and his co-host Al Hunt argued that impeachment would be a waste of time and Democrats should devote their energy to investigating the president instead. "I’ll tell you one thing that I think Democrats should steer clear of, and that’s impeachment," Hunt said. "It’s not that Trump has not committed impeachable offenses, far worse than what he was accused of back in 2019 with Ukraine. I mean, he has. I mean, you could come up with a bill of particulars of, you know, a dozen at least. But you know something, James? It’s not going to happen, and it is a distraction." "It is a waste of energy," Hunt, like other Democrats, warned further. "Investigate, investigate, investigate. Don’t go on a mission that isn’t going to succeed." JACK SMITH'S TRUMP PROBE SWEPT UP FOX NEWS, OTHER MEDIA COMMUNICATIONS AS INVESTIGATION WENT BEYOND LAWMAKERS Carville agreed, arguing that the Supreme Court is protecting Trump from the consequences of his actions. "So, you investigate, and, of course, what you’re going to find — and you’re going to find it quickly — is overwhelming evidence of criminal activity. Now, of course, he can’t commit a crime according to the Supreme Court because, well, he’s above the law," Carville lamented. "But suppose you say, ‘This is incontrovertible proof. We got to do something about this. How can he stay in office?’ And impeachment would be a very difficult thing," Carville warned. "It’s time-consuming. It’s highly unlikely to be anything because of the — you need so many votes in the Senate. But we’re going to find out a whole bunch of stuff really fast at the beginning of the year 2027. I promise you." "Well, I agree. I might quibble with ‘very fast’ because I think investigations got to be thorough. They got to be really — some of them are actually going to take a while," Hunt replied. "They’re going to build a case, but we’re going to find them out. You’re absolutely right about that. And I am only against impeachment because I think it’s not going to succeed and will be a distraction." OUTGOING HOUSE DEMOCRAT AL GREEN FILES ANOTHER IMPEACHMENT RESOLUTION TARGETING PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP Fox News Digital spoke to former Democratic advisor Dan Turrentine, who suggested Carville and Hunt are spot-on. "Al and James are right. To paraphrase James, it’s a simple math issue, stupid. Unless something truly unimaginable [happens], there will not be 67 votes in the Senate to convict. And the public is not there, either," Turrentine said. "If we win the majority, the voters that delivered it are clear, they want us laser focused on their lives, the issues they care about. We should conduct appropriate oversight and let history and 2028 be the accountability. articles.title: Former German spy chief arrested on suspicion of treason and espionage
articles.summary: August Hanning’s former chief of staff was also arrested on suspicion of ‘aiding and abetting attempted treason’.
articles.body:
Germany’s former foreign spy chief has been arrested on suspicion of espionage and treason, prosecutors have said.

August Hanning, 80, is under investigation for attempted treason and acting as an agent for a foreign intelligence service, the Office of the Federal Public Prosecutor General confirmed on Tuesday.

Hanning was president of Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service between 1998 and 2005.

He was arrested in Bad Toelz-Wolfratshausen in southern Germany. His former chief of staff, partially identified as Manfred D, was arrested in Steinfurt in western Germany on suspicion of “aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage”.

The prosecutor’s office said, “On one occasion, Hanning used classified intelligence provided by Manfred D to draft an analysis for an officer of a foreign intelligence service.”

Prosecutors said Manfred D also served as the chief of staff for Hanning’s successors between 2012 and 2026, and used his role to gain access to confidential information which he then passed on to Hanning “in exchange for remuneration”. Hanning then used the information in his private consulting work, prosecutors added.

“The current findings suggest that, over the years, Manfred D provided Hanning with approximately 2,000 documents, many of which contained classified information to be used exclusively by the federal intelligence service for internal purposes, particularly for executive intelligence briefings,” the statement said.

The statement did not reveal who the two men were suspected of spying for or which country the foreign agent worked for, adding that “it has yet to be determined if the material reached the intended recipient”.

German MP Marc Henrichmann told the AFP news agency that Germany “will not tolerate the betrayal of secrets”.

Henrichmann, who chairs the German parliament’s intelligence oversight committee, said, “Whoever allies themselves with the enemies of our liberal democracy will be found out.”

The premises of Manfred D and Hanning were being searched in several locations, including in the capital, Berlin.

articles.title: Paramount takes over Warner Bros in $110bn Hollywood merger
articles.summary: The merger of two of Hollywood's biggest movie studios comes after months of legal disputes and concern over competition.
articles.body:
Paramount Skydance has officially taken over Warner Bros Discovery in a $110bn merger that is set to reshape Hollywood and the media landscape.

The takeover - merging two of the biggest studios in Los Angeles - comes after months of legal disputes and widespread criticism over feared cuts and consolidation could harm competition and consumers.

It will alter streaming for millions, usher in a new chapter in the film and TV industry, and leave one of the biggest US news outlets, CNN, in uncertain territory.

The merger will also bring together a host of entities including HBO, CBS, Nickelodeon, Showtime, Comedy Central, DC Studios and Food Network.

Paramount will acquire ownership of iconic franchises that include Harry Potter, Game of Thrones, The Lord of the Rings and Mission: Impossible.

The newly merged entertainment behemoth will be re-branded under the name Skydance Corporation, the company originally founded by David Ellison before he took over both Paramount and Warner Bros Discover.

Ellison, chairman and chief executive of Skydance, said the completion of the deal was "historic" for the film industry.

"From the start, our ambition was to bring these two storied studios together and create a stronger competitor, with the talent, resources, and reach to tell great stories in every genre, on every platform, for audiences everywhere. Now that ambition is a reality," he said.

Films and streaming prices - how the Warner Bros deal could affect you

Last week, Ellison named the outgoing chief executive of Mattel, Ynon Kreiz, as co-chief executive.

Kreiz will focus on the company's day-to-day operations, including integrating the newly-combined businesses, while Ellison will focus on strategy and technology.

Mark Thompson - who once served as director general of the BBC - will continue in his role as chairman and editor-in-chief of CNN Worldwide, while Bari Weiss remains editor-in-chief of CBS News.

Casey Bloys, who has lead HBO and Max Content, will be the co-chair and chief content officer for direct-to-consumer content.

Mike Proulx, research director at Forrester Research, said that change "essentially means the HBO leadership team is now in charge of Skydance's combined streaming operation".

"While that bodes well for the HBO brand, make no mistake, Bloys will be pressured to find and deliver cost efficiencies that could affect content quality," he warned.

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said the company has high debts at a time when interest rates are high.

"The combined entity, now called Skydance, needs to cut costs and make bigger profits to be able to get the debt down to more manageable levels," he said.

"The fact Tom Cruise movie Digger, Warner Bros' last release before the merger, has been a major flop is a reminder of how the film industry is not a guaranteed ticket to riches."

While the company said it had received unanimous approval from competition authorities across the world, the long running takeover process has featured controversy since the beginning.

Netflix initially had a deal to buy part of Warner Bros Discovery, but Paramount Skydance launched a bidding war, leading to the streaming giant walking away.

Lawyers in about a dozen US states then filed lawsuits - led by California - aiming to block the deal, arguing it would stifle competition, raise consumer prices and cause "substantial" harm to movie theatres, cable distributors and "ultimately, audiences nationwide".

US states announced a settlement with Paramount and Ellison last month which paved the way for the merger to go ahead .

As part of the deal, Paramount has agreed to establish a "news editorial independence board" to "ensure independent, objective, fact-based reporting" at CNN and CBS.

Politics and editorial independence has become an area of concern at CBS since the news broadcaster was taken over in 2025 as part of separate a merger between Skydance Media and Paramount.

Ellison, who hosted a dinner for President Donald Trump earlier this year, has sought to reassure people that editorial independence will be maintained.

Over its 103-year-old history, Warner Bros has won more than 100 Academy Awards - including dominating at last year's show with a record-tying 11 Oscars for One Battle After Another, Sinners and Weapons.

Paramount traces its roots back 1912 and also boasts more than 100 Oscars for classics spanning from The Godfather to Titanic, though the studio has not mirrored the same recent spate of Hollywood honours.

The studio was not nominated for any projects last year by the Academy. Its last win came in 2022 with Top Gun: Maverick.

The deal with US states aims to ensure the merged studios will produce "real, robust movies" that will generate economic activity and put people back to work, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta, who led the lawsuit and settlement.

To prevent the studio from fulfilling its annual quota with low-budget or automated content, the deal includes strict guardrails against "AI-generated" films.

As part of the agreement, Paramount must release at least 30 films each year. If it fails to meet its annual production quota, it will be forced to sell its 49% stake in Miramax, the film company founded by disgraced Hollywood mogul Harvey Weinstein and his brother Bob.

Paramount also must ensure 20% of all film production takes place in the US for the first two years, rising to more than 30% through the following three years.

articles.title: China’s long-term finances are all wet as bill to maintain huge navy comes due in 2031
articles.summary: Xi Jinping's navy faces a sustainment wall by 2031 as maintenance costs collide with China's cracking fiscal system and collapsing land sales.
articles.body: China’s recent state visit bought two months of trade peace. But it did not buy Beijing time on the fleet it has already launched and will soon be unable to afford. Chinese President Xi Jinping walked a red carpet in Washington for his first state visit to the United States in more than a decade. President Donald Trump greeted him at Joint Base Andrews. There were troop reviews, a state dinner, pandas, an artificial intelligence (AI) "dialogue" and a two-month extension of a trade truce now set to expire Jan. 10. Xi told the cameras the two powers "should coexist in peace." He also pressed Trump to handle Taiwan with "prudence" and oppose independence. On the minerals that make missiles, drones and warships work, Beijing’s readout went silent. The White House said only that the two sides would "continue to work on" rare-earth shortages — practically meaning America will press hard to address its supply vulnerabilities. TRUMP-XI REUNION COMES WITH UNFINISHED BUSINESS — AND A BIGGER BATTLE LOOMING Beyond the pleasantries in Washington — it costs little to be polite and talk is far cheaper than war — China continues to press forward on a war footing, launching warships at a breathtaking pace. Communist China’s problem is no longer whether it can build a navy. It built one. The problem is whether it can keep one after 2031. IS THE US ALREADY LOSING TO CHINA ON INNOVATION, LOGISTICS AND RAPID RESUPPLY? Procurement is the cheap year. Operations and maintenance are not cheap. For a modern navy, operating and support costs commonly consume 60% to 70% of a ship’s life-cycle cost. The People’s Liberation Army Navy spent a decade in series production: destroyers, frigates, carriers, conventional and nuclear submarines. But if overhaul rates on these new ships resemble the old ones, the heaviest work on China’s most capable surface combatants begins around 2031 and runs for a decade. This will force repair yards to compete with new-build demand. The maintenance workforce is already stretched. Fuel, munitions and realistic training hours add considerably to the cost. That bill lands on a fiscal system already cracking at the local level. In 21 provincial-level regions, local revenue covers less than half of spending. Land sales, the main source of provincial income, have collapsed. Beijing has spent two years swapping "hidden" local debt onto official books, which lowered interest rates and raised the visible pile. Interest is now a hard claim on weak cash flow. Beijing can still issue bonds and order state banks to roll paper. But it cannot restore 2010s’ growth or a healthy property market. Deflation makes every yuan of debt heavier. History has seen this movie. In the 1930s, German Minister of the Economy Hjalmar Schacht hid Nazi rearmament behind Mefo bills — phony promissory notes a shell company issued so the official deficit looked respectable — and stayed hidden from the requirements of the Versailles treaty. By late 1938, the trick was exhausted. The first bills were coming due. Schacht warned that arms spending would have to be cut or the Reich would go broke. Adolf Hitler fired him. What kept Germany solvent afterward was loot: Austria, then Czechoslovakia’s gold and Skoda arms works, then Poland. Plunder postponed insolvency. Xi is not running a Mefo scheme. Local-government financing vehicles were built to pave roads and hit GDP targets, not to conceal a Versailles-illegal Wehrmacht. The parallel that matters is the maturity date. A built force starts to demand a flow of money the buildup years did not require. Hitler could rob neighbors. Xi cannot cash a Czech National Bank. He can try coercion, blockade or a short, violent fait accompli against Taiwan before the sustainment wall arrives — and before American industry finishes rerouting the supply chains his predecessors spent 20 years capturing. CHINA’S GRIP ON RARE-EARTH MAGNETS COULD CRUSH US DRONE INDUSTRY BEFORE IT GROWS That is why China’s rare-earth squeeze play looks early. China still refines the overwhelming share of the magnets used inside U.S. and allied weapons. Beijing tightened licenses, then blacklisted American firms standing up mines and magnet plants. The concept aimed to freeze the West’s rearmament while the PLA finished its own. But Trump treated the squeeze as the warning it was. Capital has rapidly moved to address the supply chain vulnerability. The Pentagon is pushing Chinese magnets out of defense supply chains, rendering America far less helpless by 2031 than it was in 2024. Every year Xi waits to use this new navy, China’s chokehold on America weakens. But if overhaul rates on these new ships resemble the old ones, the heaviest work on China’s most capable surface combatants begins around 2031 and runs for a decade. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION The recent pageantry should not confuse anyone. Xi asked Washington to go quiet on Taiwan, yet earned no policy change. He offered no real minerals deal. He settled for a two-month extension and a photo under the chandeliers. The Chinese Communist Party has centralized power, purged the officer corps and launched a modern and massive fleet — one that will be increasingly expensive to keep in five years. America should spend the next five years as if he knows it. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM CHUCK DEVORE

articles.title: Russia says no plague found in contacts of Siberian lab worker who died
articles.summary: Plague had not been detected among close contacts of a worker in an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia who died last week, with 60% of the identified group tested so far, officials in Russia said Tuesday.
articles.body: Plague had not been detected among close contacts of a worker in an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia who died last week, with 60% of the identified group tested so far, officials in Russia said Tuesday. News from Russia’s consumer and health watchdog on Sunday that a female staffer at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East had died from a “pneumonia of undetermined” origin last week has raised public health fears worldwide. “Laboratory testing identified two cases of Covid-19 and two cases of rhinovirus infection,” watchdog Rospotrebnadzor said in a statement, referring to the virus that causes the common cold. “No other infectious disease pathogens were detected among the contacts,” the statement said, without mentioning the word “plague.” Regional and national Russian authorities have not confirmed that plague was involved in the woman’s death. But American officials have urged more transparency from Moscow, with a State Department spokesperson saying Monday there had been “reports of a fatal case of suspected pneumonic plague” in Irkutsk oblast. The World Health Organization, which oversees global public health matters, said Tuesday that Russian health officials had informed the agency in response to its request on the lab worker’s death that no case of plague has been recorded in Irkutsk. “According to the authorities, the woman’s illness initially presented as a typical acute respiratory viral infection,” it said. No case of plague or other high threat pathogen has reportedly been found among the woman’s close contacts, the WHO said, quoting the response from the Russian officials, adding that it’s awaiting confirmation from the Russian side about “what pneumonia-causing pathogen had led to the individual’s death.” On Friday, Maksim Modin, mayor of the Shelekhov municipal district near the border with Mongolia, said that the inpatient facility where the worker is said to have been treated had been closed for quarantine. Russian media cited officials saying that nearly 200 people who had been in contact with the woman had been placed under precautionary medical observation. Russian media outlets have named the woman and identified her as being 28 years old. These details have not been announced by officials. Irkutsk’s governor, Igor Kobsev, said Monday that no “microorganisms linked to the employee’s professional activities were detected” in her body. The Irkutsk regional branch of Rospotrebnadzor on Tuesday denied what it called “fake” reports circulating online that an “enhanced sanitary-epidemiological regime” and strict restrictions have been imposed in the region. “No such decisions have been made at this time,” it said in a statement, saying the situation in the region remains stable. Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Monday that even though there is “very limited travel between the U.S. and Russia,” if “something like that gets out, it could quickly spread.” President Donald Trump told reporters Monday the United States would do what it could to help Russia. “I hate to see them having it,” Trump said. “It’s a rough disease.” Meanwhile, some of Russia’s neighbors have been stepping up preventive measures and quarantine controls at border crossings. The Kremlin has called for those concerned to heed official statements. “Rospotrebnadzor provides comprehensive information,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said when reporters pressed him about rumors spreading amid sparse official statements. Peskov also deferred to Rospotrebnadzor when asked if the worker’s lab results would be released or if an autopsy has been conducted. On its website, the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute of Siberia and the Far East says it was founded in 1934 “as a scientific and operational body for combating plague,” but over the years, its scope of responsibility expanded to include “other highly dangerous diseases,” including cholera and anthrax. The institute says it’s a “multidisciplinary research and anti-epidemic facility” that helps ensure epidemic safety in the region.

Lab workers at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, in an undated photo. via AP
The headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, in Moscow on Monday. Igor Ivanko / AFP via Getty

articles.title: Defence lawyer in Cornell University case calls for special prosecutor Letitia James to be removed
articles.summary: New York Attorney General Letitia James is investigating the rape allegations, but the lawyer says comments she made on the case should disqualify her.
articles.body:
A lawyer for one of the seven men accused of participating in a Cornell University gang rape has called for the special prosecutor on the case to recuse herself over past public comments.

The lawyer had said a social media post from New York Attorney General Letitia James throws into question her investigation's "integrity and independence".

In the 28 September post, James wrote that "what this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable" and told survivors that "we stand with you".

The university's administration is under fire over its alleged mishandling of the October 2024 incident and, according to US media, now faces a no-confidence vote by Cornell faculty.

The university's Faculty Senate, a governing body comprised of professors and other academic staff, will vote on a resolution of no confidence next week, according to reports. Cornell is an Ivy League university, alongside Harvard and Yale, and its faculty includes Nobel laureates and other distinguished researchers.

A majority no-confidence vote would be a largely symbolic gesture, signalling the broader faculty's discontent and applying pressure on university leadership to act.

The BBC has reached out to Cornell University for comment.

Allegations made in a lawsuit against seven men and the university have rocked the campus in New York state, with hundreds of students and faculty members gathering there on Monday in protest, and sparked anger across the country.

New York Governor Kathy Hochul last week appointed James as a special prosecutor to investigate the case and how law enforcement and the university initially responded to the allegations made by a woman identified in the lawsuit as Jane Doe.

Jane Doe has accused the university of failing to protect her, after she was allegedly drugged and raped by the men for several hours at a fraternity party.

Days before she was appointed special prosecutor, James wrote on X: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable.

"I'm holding her in my heart and in my prayers," she continued. "To her, and to all survivors: you're not alone. We stand with you."

The lawyer for one of the seven accused said these remarks were disqualifying.

In a statement sent to the BBC's US media partner, CBS News, the lawyer said her comments conflict with the need for "independently evaluating the evidence".

"This is not an accusation that Attorney General James is corrupt, acting in bad faith or incapable of performing her duties professionally," the statement said.

"Nor am I suggesting that a court has determined that she is legally disqualified. The point is much narrower: an avoidable question now hangs over this investigation, and voluntary recusal would remove it."

Governor Hochul and James were questioned about impartiality concerns during a news conference, and Hochul said James would "follow the facts".

"She'll examine the evidence and go wherever it leads, and if the evidence supports charges, she will pursue them," Hochul said.

articles.title: Cornell protesters swarm campus to support Jane Doe, call for university president's resignation
articles.summary: Cornell University faculty push a no confidence vote as student protests erupt over sexual assault allegations tied to a fraternity lawsuit.
articles.body: Faculty at Cornell University are weighing a vote of no confidence in the school's administration as student protesters take over the campus in response to sexual assault allegations on Tuesday. The no-confidence resolution has secured support from 40 of the faculty senate's 75 voting members, according to the resolution's sponsor, professor Paul Ortiz. "As you may suspect, we were approached in our capacity as faculty senators by numerous Cornell colleagues demanding action. Many of these faculty – including myself – were approached by students at Cornell who are upset, fearful for their personal safety, and wanting our university to address the perennial problem of sexual assault on the campus," Ortiz wrote. AOC'S DRAMATIC RETELLING OF CORNELL RAPE ALLEGATIONS COLLIDES WITH COMPLAINT DETAILS Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff also faced questions from the student body during a campus assembly on Monday as protests took over the college. "We’re not hiding anything at Cornell," Kotlikoff told students, according to the Cornell Daily Sun student newspaper. "You will hear proposals from us going forward around what we’re going to do to try and improve this culture and address this problem." Kotlikoff has so far dismissed student calls for his resignation. CORNELL CAMPUS POLICE MADE DRUG ARREST AT CHI PHI FRATERNITY HOUSE HOURS BEFORE ALLEGED GANG RAPE Seven former Chi Phi fraternity brothers are accused in a lawsuit of drugging and raping a female Cornell student during a night of drinking, drugs and group sex at their fraternity house in October 2024. The accuser, identified in court papers by the pseudonym Jane Doe, alleges the men sexually assaulted her after she arrived intoxicated and was pressured into taking ketamine and other substances. The men have denied wrongdoing, with some maintaining the sexual activity was consensual and others denying they participated in it. No criminal charges have been filed against the seven men. ATTORNEY FOR ACCUSED CORNELL STUDENT CALLS ON LETITIA JAMES TO STEP ASIDE OVER PRIOR COMMENTS The case has now erupted into a political and legal firestorm, with New York Attorney General Letitia James announcing Friday that her office is conducting an "active criminal investigation" after Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed the Office of the Attorney General as special prosecutor. Cornell has separately agreed to retain outside counsel to conduct an independent review of the university's handling of the allegations. At the center of the controversy are sharply conflicting accounts of what happened that night, including differences between what Doe said in the weeks afterward, what prosecutors say they received from Cornell police and the explosive allegations contained in a lawsuit filed nearly two years later.
